hvytrkdvmt.name: HvyTrkDvmt
hvytrkdvmt.description: Average daily vehicle miles of travel on roadways in the region by heavy trucks during the base year. The value for this input may be NA instead of number. In that case, if a state abbreviation is provided, the base year value is calculated from the state per capita rate tabulated by the LoadDefaultRoadDvmtValues.R script and the base year population. If the state abbreviation is NA (as for a metropolitan model) the base year value is calculated from metropolitan area per capita rates and metropolitan area population.

The name(s) must be consistent with names in the urbanized area names in the default data. See module documentation for a listing.

azone_carsvc_characteristics.html:
File 01_azone_carsvc_characteristics

May 21, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that azone_carsvc_characteristics has five attributes:

The first two attributes are the average cost per mile for a “high level” and “low level” car service, respectively, with the input data suggesting to the research team that the former is in an urban location with lots of competing car services and the latter is in a more rural location where per-mile car service would be more expensive.

The third attribute is the average age of vehicles in the car service fleet in years.

The last two attributes are the proportion of light truck owners, and then car owners, who would substitute a lower-cost car service option for their vehicle.

For example, these data suggest that the costs per mile in Charlottesville and Albemarle are $2.16 in areas of high level car service and $3.73 per mile in areas of low level car service, with an average vehicle age of 5 years. Further, if the car service price is lower than vehicle ownership costs, then 55% of all car owners and 45% of light truck owners would switch to the car service according to the model.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval using this file is to evaluate how changes in the cost or attractiveness of car service (e.g., ride-hailing, taxis, or pooled mobility) influence household vehicle ownership and travel behavior. As described in Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development, reducing the generalized cost of car service—particularly lower-cost service tiers—can increase the likelihood that households substitute away from private vehicle ownership.

Within the model, this substitution effect operates through the LtTrkCarSvcSubProp and AutoCarSvcSubProp parameters, which represent behavioral elasticities linking car service availability to vehicle ownership decisions. Lower car service costs or higher substitution proportions can reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT), increase shared trips, and shift mode choice toward more efficient transportation options, with downstream impacts on congestion and emissions.

Method Used for Virginia

Costs per mile

Examination of one site (https://taxis-fare.com/uber-fare-state-virginia) showed a per-mile cost of $1.75 per km, but to the research team’s surprise, this cost was the same in three locations—urban Arlington, rural Bristol, and very rural Highland County. Then, using the Uber site directly, a 7.7 mile trip in (rural) Highland County had a price of $1.92 per mile and a 2.9 mile trip in (urban) Alexandria had a cost of $5.84 per mile—which is precisely the opposite of what one would expect (e.g., one would expect higher costs in the more rural area).

The reason for this discrepancy appears to be twofold. First, in urban areas, one may also have more congestion, and while distance is a factor in pricing, another factor is the trip duration. Second, delay in waiting for a vehicle also varies and is not reflected in the price. Rather, for the rural location, the website noted a “longer wait”, whereas for the urban location the website noted a vehicle was available in 5 minutes. Interestingly, this ratio $5.84 versus $1.92 per mile (all in 2026 dollars) is almost identical to the ratio used by the Rogue Valley MPO (which gave per-mile costs of $1 and $3 per mile), except that for RVMPO, the high car service level yielded the lower number ($1) as one would expect.

Another site, //www.taxifarefinder.com/rates.php, showed per-mile costs of $2.60 (urban location of Alexandria), $2.16 (less but still urban location of Fairfax), and $2.10 (Roanoke), and then for rural Highland County, gave a cost of $3.73 per mile—that is, a higher fare for the rural area.

For now, the research team used the $2.16 cost per mile or high car service areas and then the $3.73 cost per mile for low service areas, thinking that on balance, the theory should hold and that the examination of sites on a single day yields limited information. That said, users can adjust these for their own location, with one option being to make them the same amount.

Vehicle age

The average age of all passenger (class 1-2) vehicles in Virginia was estimated as at least 8 years, based on data from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (2023). (The full citation is: U.S. Department of Transportation, Bureau of Transportation Statistics; and U.S. Department of Commerce, Census Bureau. (2023-10-02). Vehicle Stats by State, Vehicle Type, and GVWR. 2021 Vehicle Inventory and Use Survey.https://www.bts.gov/browse-statistical-products-and-data/surveys/vius/vehicle-stats-state-vehicle-type-and-gvwr.) This calculation presumes the data were collected in 2022; the number of vehicles are given by model year for each of the years 2012-2021 and then the total number of vehicles for 2011 or earlier are given as one figure. For this last category, the research team used 12 years (e.g., 2022-2010 as a value that would presumably eliminate very old vehicles from being used for a carsharing service).

That said, one would expect the average age of a carsharing service vehicle, such as Uber or Lyft, to either be 8 years (the average of all vehicles) or some lower number. For now the team used a value of 5 years, but presumably any value between 0 and 8 would be reasonable if one expected for-hire vehicles to be less than or equal to the average age of all vehicles (class 1-2, excluding trucks).

Proportion of owners who would use a carsharing vehicle

The research team did not have a solid way of determining the proportion of owners (cars or light trucks) who would use a carsharing service in lieu of a privately-owned vehicle. The proportion should presumably not be 1.0, because there will be locations where carsharing service levels are poor and there is a delay to get a ride. One would also expect this percentage to be lower for light trucks to the extent that light trucks are used for commercial purposes. The team has chosen values of 0.55 (cars) and 0.45 (light trucks) for these two proportions, respectively, but other values can be justified.

azone_charging_availability.html:
File 02_azone_charging_availability

April 12, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file contains information on charging availability with respect to three proportions. The guidance notes two very different indications for the first proportion and the latter two.

PropSFChargingAvail is the proportion of single-family dwelling units where EV charging facilities exist or can be installed

By contrast, the other two proportions, PropMFChargingAvail and PropGQChargingAvail, are the proportion of multifamily dwelling units and group quarters dwelling units that already have charging facilities available.

For example, the data below suggest that 58% of single family detached dwelling units in Albemarle County and Charlottesville City can support charging of electric vehicles, compared to 30% of apartments and 25% of college dormitories or other types of group quarters. The baseline case is that these percentages will not change by 2045.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changes in charging availability may affect fuel consumption, emissions, or DVMT (if it is the case that VMT in an electric vehicle differs from VMT in a conventional vehicle). The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, explains that “Users can explore policies that may expand or reduce EV ownership in the model region, and how those may impact emissions or DVMT goals. Additionally, users can explore how changes in the energy profile or policies may impact EV emissions and charging.”

For example, the U.S. Department of Energy (https://afdc.energy.gov/fuels/electricity-charging-multi) reports that homeowners associations and building managers can take steps to support charging stations. A scenario could envision that if these steps were taken such that the proportion of multifamily units with charging stations increased from 30% to some other value, what would be the impact on emissions or fuel consumed?

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year

There are a variety of literature sources regarding EV charging facilities but the research team did not find sources that gives these numbers for individual cities. Rather, the following approach was used:

For single family dwelling units, the research team used a figure of 58%, which was reported by Inside EVs (2021) as the number of houses that could support a charger based on the fact that they have a garage. Having a garage does not necessarily mean a house can support a charger as the wiring in the home must be ready (and indeed an outdoor plug without a garage can support a charger with proper wiring).

For multifamily charging the research team placed this percentage for all Azones at 30%. This was based on a report by Kuby et al. (2025), which stated that two other studies had estimated that “the percentage of MFH [multi-family housing] residents with access to 120V and awareness that they could charge an EV with it is 2–5%, although more optimistic scenarios increase this percentage to 19–48 %.” Based solely on Kuby et al. (2025), one could argue that any percentage between 19% and 48% could be justified; the research team chose 30% as a lower range midpoint value.

For group quarters (e.g., dormitories, skilled facilities, the research team used a value of 25% as a baseline case.) This answer will vary both by location and by the number of chargers at a given location (e.g., level 1 versus level 2 chargers and number of vehicles per charger). An answer of higher than 40% could be supported based on a review of the University of Illinois (undated) for college dormitories alone.

Forecast Year

At the time of some Virginia VisionEval work published in 2022 (https://vtrc.virginia.gov/media/vtrc/vtrc-pdf/vtrc-pdf/22-R21.pdf), researchers used sources such as the Department of Energy and the U.S. Energy Information Administration to make forecasts of electric vehicle use, and certainly such forecasts could be used to estimate charging availability in 2045. However, events that have transpired suggest that one possibly should not assume that charging infrastructure will necessarily increase. Thus regional planners may have the 2045 business as usual scenario represent some increase in charging availability since 2024—or it may be reasonable to presume that the values in 2045 are the same as those in 2024 (and thus a scenario could be to look at how increases in such availability affects EV use). For this statewide file, the research team made the base case that 2045 values are the same as 2024 values.

Appendix

Kuby, M., Cordova-Cruzatty, A., Parker, N.C., and King, D.A. King. EV Charging for Multifamily Housing: Review of Evidence, Methods, Barriers, and Opportunities, Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews, Volume 210, March 2025, 115253.

azone_electricity_carbon_intensity.html:
Optional File 03_azone_electricity_carbon_intensity

May 31, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) uses this optional file to define the greenhouse gas emissions associated with electricity consumption. This is measured in grams of CO₂ equivalent per megajoule (gCO₂e/MJ). This file is not required—the user can simply omit it from the base run if desired. If the user chooses to use this file, the primary advantage is to tailor the output to local conditions. For example, the data below suggest that in year 2024, Albemarle will generate 87.3 gCO₂e per MJ of electricity, but year 2045 will see this value drop to 70.8 gCO₂e.

Possible Scenario

One primary scenario in VisionEval using this input is to examine how the decarbonization of the electrical grid influences the total greenhouse gas (GHG) reduction benefits of transitioning to electric vehicles.

As noted in A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, users can explore how aggressive renewable energy mandates (like those in the Virginia Clean Economy Act) impact the "upstream" emissions of transportation. Lowering the carbon intensity value reflects a cleaner grid, which maximizes the environmental benefits of high EV adoption rates.

Method Used for Virginia

The EPA provides a greenhouse gas equivalencies calculator (https://www.epa.gov/energy/greenhouse-gas-equivalencies-calculator) for which one may enter a zip code and the number of kilowatt-hours used and one is returned the number of grams of CO2 equivalent. For each zip code, the research team entered 277.8 kwH as an input (which is equal to 1,000 MJ) and then as an output received the number of kgCO₂e; thus this number represented the number of grams per 1 MJ. (For example, for zip code 22003, entering the value of 277.8 kwh (which is 1,000 MJ) yields 82.7 kg of CO₂e; this means 87.2 g of CO₂e per 1 MJ).

The file https://genguide.com.ng/complete-list-of-all-virginia-zip-codes/ provides over 825 zip codes for Virginia’s cities and counties. For each city or county, the team choose the zip code with the largest population and used that in the calculator.

Almost all of the Azones had one of two values: 82.7 g of CO₂e per MJ or 133 g of CO₂e per MJ. (The three two exceptions were Lee County [124] and Accomack and Northampton Counties [87.3]. One reason for these differences appears to be that some regions in Virginia rely on natural gas power plants (see https://cleanview.co/power-projects/operating/natural-gas-power-plants/virginia) whereas other regions in Virginia rely on coal plants (see https://cleanview.co/power-projects/operating/coal-power-plants/virginia). Another reason may be differences in the extent to which these sources rely on solar and/or wind in addition to fossil fuel sources.

Forecasting changes for year 2045 entails some uncertainty. There are numerous online sources, one of which is from the Congressional Budget Office which in, 2022 (https://www.cbo.gov/system/files/2022-12/58419-co2-emissions-elec-power.pdf) forecast on printed page 12 several possible reductions in greenhouse gases from the electric power sector to year 2050. Two sets of reductions (High, reference or midcase, and low) were given—one for the situation prior to the 2022 budget reconciliation act and one following that situation. Factors influencing any actual reductions include shifts away from coal-fired plants, use of renewable sources such as solar and wind, and advances in battery technology; the graphs also underscore the relevance of public policy. For 2045, the research team applied a reduction of 14.3%, based on a reading of the 2045 reference case (1.4 billion metric tons) to the 2024 case (1.2 billion metric tons) prior to the budget reconciliation. For example, a figure of 82.7 g CO2e per MJ was used in 2024 for Amelia County. For 2045, this value is 70.9 g CO2e per MJ. Users can adjust these assumptions for changes specific to their region; for example, for a region using a coal power plant at present but which is planning a transition to natural gas in the next decade, then a much larger reduction would be applicable.

Appendix—Another Method

(Note that in the above calculations, single statewide value for the SERC egrid region covering North Carolina and Virginia, available at https://www.epa.gov/energy/greenhouse-gas-equivalencies-calculator-calculations-and-references, indicates 623 pounds of CO₂e per mWH which is 623* 453.59237 grams of CO₂e per mWH or 623* 453.59237 grams of CO₂e per 3600 MJ which is 78.5 grams of CO₂e per MJ—a value that is lower than those shown in this file. It appears that the reason is that the EPA calculator provides a marginal value rather than an average value; thus users could elect to reduce the figures shown slightly but the more critical element appears to be determining which region’s figures are applicable—that is, the value for the region containing Cumberland is substantially different from the value for the region containing Dickenson).

An alternative approach for future consideration is to explore the EPA AVERT Web Edition tool( AVERT Web Edition | US EPA AVERT provides regionally specific emissions estimates from the electric grid. The data may be developed as follows where one uses the Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) which was calculated based on current grid data and projected decarbonization trends. These figures allow the model to estimate the carbon footprint of electric vehicle (EV) charging and household electricity use over time.

:

Step 1: Identify the AVERT Region Virginia lies within the Eastern U.S. AVERT regions, primarily the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast grid zones. The selection reflects actual power consumed by households and businesses within the Commonwealth, accounting for local generation and regional imports.

Step 2: Establish the Base Year (2024) Using 2024 emissions outputs normalized by energy delivered, one estimate converted this intensity was converted to 57 gCO₂e/MJ, which is lower than the values shown previously. This represents the baseline carbon footprint of the Virginia grid.

Step 3: Project the Target Year (2045) To capture long-term policy impacts—including the retirement of coal units and the expansion of solar and wind—a 2045 projection is needed. Different sets of assumptions will yield different results. For example, one set of assumptions was modeled using AVERT’s clean energy adoption assumptions. This resulted in a projected intensity of 14 gCO₂e/MJ, consistent with deep decarbonization pathways used in EPA and DOE scenario work.

Step 4: Apply to Virginia Geographies. VisionEval requires values for each Azone (95 counties and 38 independent cities). The grid is managed regionally rather than by municipality, so ideally one would consider these different regions. That said, this approach could yield the same statewide values (57 for 2024; 14 for 2045) for all Azones.

Sources for the Appendix are:

EPA AVERT Web Edition Tool. U.S. Environmental Protection Agency. https://www.epa.gov/avert/avert-web-edition

azone_fuel_power_cost.html:
File 04_azone_fuel_power_cost.csv

April 9, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-azone_fuel_power_cost.csv) defines azone_fuel_power_cost.csv as providing the retail cost of fuel and electricity used in the CalculateVehicleOperatingCost module. These costs are key inputs for estimating household vehicle operating expenses by azone.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changes in fuel and electricity prices influence household travel behavior, vehicle operating costs, and energy consumption. Adjustments to these prices may affect vehicle miles traveled, vehicle type choice (e.g., ICE vs. electric), and overall transportation expenditures. For example, increases in fuel prices may lead households to reduce discretionary travel, shift to more fuel-efficient vehicles, or increase adoption of alternative modes such as transit, walking, or biking. Lower fuel prices may encourage additional discretionary driving and higher vehicle miles traveled. Changes in electricity prices may similarly influence the relative cost of operating electric vehicles, potentially affecting the rate of EV adoption or usage.

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

The file compiles two primary cost components: retail fuel prices (gasoline and diesel) and electricity prices. These values are used to estimate per-mile operating costs for different vehicle types across all azones. The dataset includes both a base year and a forecast year for these two prices.

Initial Calculations

Fuel price data were obtained from the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA), specifically the Weekly Retail Gasoline and Diesel Prices dataset. Units for fuel prices are $/gallon, including taxes.

Electricity price data were sourced from the EIA’s Electric Sales, Revenue, and Average Price dataset. Units for electricity prices are $/kWh.

Fuel Costs

Fuel cost data reflect values for 2024. Because the file structure includes year-specific field names, both base year and future year values must be expressed in constant (2024) dollars.

To estimate the target year values, historical fuel price trends and price index data from the model’s deflator (def) folder were used. While fuel prices fluctuate annually, the long-term trend is relatively stable (see below). Based on this observation, target year values were set equal to base year values in constant base year dollars. In short, we expect fuel cost growth to match overall inflation in the long run.

Fuel cost vs. Price Index (from def folder) (1999-2024).

Electricity Costs

Electricity price data reflect 2023 values. To align with the fuel cost base year, a 2024 value was projected using a 5-year compound annual growth rate (CAGR).

Base Year Projection Using 5-Year GAGR.

A similar approach to fuel costs was used for projecting 2045 values. Electricity price trends and deflator data were reviewed, and, given the consistent long-term trend (see below), target year values were set equal to base year values in constant base year dollars.Electricity Cost Growth vs. Price Index Growth (2019-2024).

Sources

- VisionEval definition of the input file: https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-azone_fuel_power_cost.csv

- VisionEval CalculateVehicleOperatingCost: https://github.com/visioneval/visioneval/blob/main/sources/modules/VETravelPerformance/inst/module_docs/CalculateVehicleOperatingCost.md

- U.S. Energy Information Administration – Weekly Retail Gasoline and Diesel Prices: https://www.eia.gov/dnav/pet/pet_pri_gnd_a_epmr_pte_dpgal_w.htm

- U.S. Energy Information Administration – Electric Sales, Revenue, and Average Price: https://www.eia.gov/electricity/sales_revenue_price/

azone_gq_pop_by_age.html:
File 05_azone_gq_pop_by_age.csv

March 26, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-azone_gq_pop_by_age.csv) defines azone_gq_pop_by_age.csv as containing the amount of people living in non-institutional group quarters, sorted by age, for each Virginia city and county. The population is divided into six age categories: 0-14, 15-19, 20-29, 30-54, 55-64, and 65 Plus. The base data used for this file came from the 2020 Census PC07 table, which reports group quarters populations in non-institutional facilities by sex and age. Institutional group quarters were excluded under the VisionEval assumption that these populations do not account for much, if any, travel.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changes in the population living in non-institutional group quarters influence travel behavior and transportation demand. Because group quarters populations (i.e. college dormitories, military barracks, and other shared living arrangements) often have different travel patterns than typical households, shifts in their size or age distribution may affect vehicle ownership rates, transit usage, and non-motorized travel. For example, an increase in younger populations (ages 15–29) in group quarters may lead to lower vehicle ownership and higher reliance on walking, biking, or transit. This file can also be used to explore how regional population growth in college towns or military areas impacts overall travel demand.

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

The file was developed in two stages. First, 2020 group quarters populations were assembled for each Virginia city and county from Census PC07 data. Male and female counts were added together and then sorted into the six VisionEval age bands used in azone_gq_pop_by_age.csv. Base year values (2024) were projected from these 2020 data. Second, 2045 values were estimated using Woods & Poole population forecasts.

Initial Calculations

To produce the 2020 values, corresponding male and female age categories from the Census PC07 table were added together and re-binned into the six VisionEval age groups. To estimate the 2045 values, we assume the relationship between group quarters population and total population within each age group will remain proportionally consistent over time. The base formula used was:

(2020 GQ population for county X / 2020 total population for county X) = (2045 GQ population for county X / 2045 total population for county X)

Because the 2020 group quarters population, the 2020 total population, and the Woods & Poole 2045 total population were all available by age group, the 2020 age-specific ratios could be applied to the 2045 totals to estimate 2045 non-institutional group quarters population by age.

When Woods & Poole grouped nearby counties and cities together, a modified version of the formula was used. For example, if City X and County X were combined in the forecast data, the estimate for City X was based on the city share of the combined city-county population in 2020 and 2045:

(2020 GQ pop. for City X) / (2020 total pop. for City X + 2020 total pop. for County X) = (2045 GQ pop. for City X) / (2045 total pop. for City X + 2045 total pop. for County X)

Revised Base Year Calculations

To project the base year (2024) values, each city/county's compound annual growth rate (CAGR) was calculated using the 2020 and 2045 values, and the 2024 values were subsequently projected.

Other Notes

Critically, VisionEval’s internal logic for the AssignLifeCycle function (see Appendix A on the following pages) cannot handle nonzero values in the GrpAge0to14 column (see Danville City above). 05_azone_gq_pop_by_age.csv includes corrected values for all GEOIDs, where any nonzero values are set to 0 to prevent error. However, we include an uncorrected version, 05_azone_gq_pop_by_age.xlsx for complete data retention. To use the uncorrected file, edit the logic for AssignLifeCycle in R before running VisionEval:

Run:

fixInNamespace("AssignLifeCycle", ns = "VESimHouseholds")

Inside function editor add:

LifeCycle_[(NumChildren_ >= 1) & (NumAdults_ == 0)] <- "03"

Appendix A

AssignLifeCycle Module

September 6, 2018

This module assigns a life cycle category to each household. The life cycle categories are similar, but not the same as, those established for the NHTS. The age categories used in VisionEval models are broader than those used by the NHTS to identify children of different ages. As a result it is not possible for the life cycle designations to reflect child ages as they do in the NHTS. Also, adulthood is determined differently in this module. The NHTS uses age 21 as the threshold age for adulthood. This module uses use 20 as nominal age break for adulthood (the 20-29 age group). Moreover, the module identifies some younger persons to be adults in situations where they are likely to be be living independently as adults or emancipated minors. Persons in the 15 to 19 age group are considered adults when there are no older adults (ages 30+) in the household.

Model Parameter Estimation

This module has no parameters. A set of rules assigns age group categories based on the age of persons and workers in the household.

How the Module Works

The module uses datasets on the numbers of persons in each household by age category and the numbers of workers by age category. The age categories are 0-14 years, 15-19 years, 20-29 years, 30-54 years, 55-64 years, and 65+ years. However no workers are in the 0-14 year age category. The household life cycle is determined by the number of children in combination with the number of adults and whether the adults are retired. The categories are as follows: 01: one adult, no children 02: 2+ adults, no children 03: one adult, children (corresponds to NHTS 03, 05, and 07) 04: 2+ adults, children (corresponds to NHTS 04, 06, and 08) 09: one adult, retired, no children 10: 2+ adults, retired, no children

Because the 15-19 age category can be ambiguous with regard to adult or child status, the status of persons in that age category in the household is determined based on the presence of older adults in the household. If there are no older persons or only persons aged 20-29 in the household, the age 15-19 persons are considered to be adults. Otherwise they are considered to be children.

The retirement status of adults is determined based on age and worker status. Households are considered to be populated with retired persons if all the adults are in the 65+ age category and there are no workers. If children are present in the household with retired persons, then the life cycle category is 03 or 04 rather than 09 or 10.

User Inputs

This module has no user input requirements.

azone_hh_av_veh_per_driver.html:
Optional File 06_azone_hh_ave_veh_per_driver.csv

June 1, 2026

Definition of the Input File

This file does not appear in the VisionEval inputs (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) and as of now does not appear to affect VisionEval results. Execution of the multimomodal module and then summing the attributes UrbanHhDvmt, TownHhDvmt, and RuralHhDvmt (found in a test file Marea_SayedMM_2045) did not show any differences for the cases of 1.1 vehicles per household, 0.1 vehicles per household, and running the file entirely. The only mention of azone_hh_ave_veh_per_driver.csv in official VisionEval documentation is the following: “Users can also use the azone_hh_ave_veh_per_driver.csv to reduce or increase vehicle ownership at the Azone level. It should be noted that this file inherently reduces the sensitivity of the AdjustVehicleOwnership module”

In the future, if this file were needed, it could be defined as shown below: the average number of vehicles per driver by azone. This input is used to estimate vehicle availability within households and plays a role in determining travel behavior and vehicle ownership patterns.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario for this input file is to examine how changes in vehicle availability per driver influence travel behavior, vehicle ownership patterns, and transportation demand. Higher vehicles per driver may indicate greater accessibility to personal vehicles, potentially increasing vehicle miles traveled and reducing reliance on alternative modes of transit. Lower vehicles per driver may reflect constraints on vehicle access, encouraging mode shifts or trip consolidation. Changes in this variable may also reflect broader societal trends such as urbanization, affordability constraints, or policy interventions aimed at reducing vehicle dependence.

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

The file was developed by combining data on the number of drivers and the number of vehicles for each azone. The ratio of vehicles to drivers was calculated to represent the average number of vehicles available per driver. Values were estimated for a base year and a future forecast year to support scenario modeling.

Initial Calculations

Driver counts were obtained from the Virginia Traffic Crash Facts report for 2023. Vehicle counts were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau Table B25046: Aggregate Number of Vehicles Available by Tenure from the 2023 ACS 5-Year Estimates. The total number of vehicles was divided by the total number of drivers for each azone to calculate an initial 2023 ratio.

Forecast Assumptions

National trends suggest that the average number of vehicles per driver is gradually declining due to factors such as increased urbanization, improved access to alternative transportation modes, and rising vehicle costs. Based on this trend and limited availability of localized forecasts, base year values were estimated by multiplying the 2023 ratios by 0.985. 2045 values were estimated by multiplying the 2023 ratios by 0.85 to reflect a continued long-term decline.

Sources- VisionEval mention: https://visioneval.github.io/docs/validation-and-troubleshooting.html

- Virginia Traffic Crash Facts Report (2023): https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/sites/default/files/documents/VA-traffic-crash-2024.pdf

- U.S. Census Bureau ACS Table B25046 (2023 5-Year Estimates): https://data.census.gov/table/ACSDT5Y2023.B25046

azone_hh_lttrk_prop.html:
07_azone_hh_lttrk_prop

May 25, 2026

Definition of the Input File

The file azone_lttrk_prop.csv specifies the proportion of household vehicles that are light trucks (pickup trucks, SUVs, and vans) within each Azone and year. This input is formally defined in the VisionEval documentation: https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#azone_lttrk_prop where the main attribute is the proportion of household vehicles classified as light trucks within each analysis zone (Azone) for each modeled year. In the VisionEval framework, passenger vehicles are bifurcated into two primary categories based on EPA MOVES classifications: Autos (SourceType 21, including sedans and coupes) and Light Trucks (SourceType 31, including pickups, SUVs, and vans).

For example, the table below suggests that in year 2024, less than half (40.7%) of vehicles in the City of Charlottesville are light duty trucks or SUVs, with this percentage being unchanged in 2045.

Possible Scenario

The proportion of light trucks is a critical driver of a region's environmental and economic profile because these vehicles typically possess different energy consumption rates and emission profiles compared to passenger cars. This file allows planners to test diverse scenarios, such as urban vehicle downsizing policies where dense areas like Alexandria City might see shifts in vehicle preference or rural demand shifts driven by functional needs in areas like Albemarle County.

For instance, a scenario might model a significant shift in consumer preference toward larger vehicles (SUVs and trucks) as they become increasingly electrified. In this case, the LtTrkProp would increase over time. By comparing a 2024 baseline to a 2045 projection, VisionEval can calculate the resulting impacts on greenhouse gas emissions, household transportation costs, and vehicle ownership decisions.

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval does not explicitly suggest that this input file lends itself to a what-if scenario. However, the document notes that vehicles in general have grown heavier, and thus a policy that might affect the proportion of such vehicles, such as a tax based on vehicle weight, could thus be developed based on this input file.

Method Used for Virginia Statewide

Base Year 2024

From the 2021 Report completed on VisionEval (22-R21.pdf), it was determined that, “It is possible to roughly estimate the proportion of household vehicles that are trucks by using vehicle populations periodically developed by the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality (Lewis-Cheatham, 2020) as part of the National Emissions Inventory. These populations are used with the EPA MOVES model and the proportion can be determined from two of the 13 MOVES vehicle types: passenger car (type 21) and passenger truck (31), the latter of which includes “many SUVs and minivans” (U.S. EPA, 2019). This approach is thus only an estimate; also there is not a perfect alignment between EPA vehicle classifications and FHWA vehicle classifications (Ponticello, 2020) with the U.S. EPA (2019) defining “light duty vehicles” based on weight and emissions. Further, it is also possible that some of these vehicles are for commercial uses rather than household uses. That said, one method for determining the inputs for this file (azone_lttrk_prop.csv) is to use the vehicle populations from the NEI. For example, in 2017, there were 467,631 passenger cars in Fairfax County (vehicle type 21 in the National Emissions Inventory) and 364,020 passenger trucks in Fairfax County (vehicle type 31), such that the proportion of trucks is 364,020 / (467,631 + 364,020) = 43.8% in 2017. This proportion was presumed to remain constant two years later in 2019 and again in 2024.

Forecast Year 2045

For 2045, there are not Virginia specific forecasts but there are national or worldwide forecasts that suggest this ratio may not necessarily remain constant. Voelk (2020) quotes an interviewee from IHS Markit who stated that in 2025, the “light-truck segment” (inclusive of SUVs and pickup trucks) was expected to increase from 72% to 78%. A graphic published in Schuster (2018) forecast that the share of SUVs sold in the U.S. would increase from 50% in 2020 to 53% in 2025. The International Energy Agency (2019) noted that worldwide use of oil attributed to growing popularity of SUVs could reduce the benefit of electrification between the present and 2040, although this worldwide forecast includes other countries where SUV use is lower than in the U.S. at present and thus has more room to increase (Schuster, 2018).

However, the passage of time (2021-2026) suggests that it is difficult to adequately apply these national forecasts to Virginia datasets. Thus this file presumes 2045 and 2024 values are the same. The user may, of course, change these values if better forecast information becomes available.

Sources

International Energy Agency. World Energy Outlook 2019, Paris, November 2019. https://iea.blob.core.windows.net/assets/1f6bf453-3317-4799-ae7b-9cc6429c81d8/English-WEO-2019-ES.pdf.

Lewis-Cheatham, S. Email to J. Ponticello, November 18, 2020.

Ponticello, J. Email to J.S. Miller, November 18, 2020.

Schuster, J. SUV Takeover. LMC Automotive, Detroit, 2018. https://lmc-auto.com/news-and-insights/segment-trends-cars-and-suvs/. Accessed November 24, 2020.

U.S. EPA. How does MOVES Classify Light-Duty Trucks? Washington, D.C., 2019. https://www.epa.gov/moves/how-does-moves-classify-light-duty-trucks. Accessed November 23, 2020.

Voel, T. “Rise of S.U.V.s: Leaving Cars in Their Dust, With No Signs of Slowing”, The New York Times, May 21, 2020. https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/21/business/suv-sales-best-sellers.html#:~:text=%E2%80%9CS.U.V.s%20made%20up%2047.4%20percent,compared%20to%2072%20percent%20now.%E2%80%9D. Accessed November 24, 2020.

SCRAP Work

The following approach illustrates some R coding that can be used in the future if one wanted to simply have siimilar values for different Azones. Ultimatlely, however, this approach was not used because we realized it is better to have individual data (which are avaialble for the base year) for each Azone. But the coding may be useful in the future, so we left it here.

library(dplyr)# Example classificationurban <- c("Arlington","Falls Church","Alexandria","Richmond City")suburban <- c("Fairfax County","Henrico","Chesterfield","Albemarle")rural <- c("Wise","Lee","Buchanan","Grayson")assign_lttrk <- function(geo){ if(geo %in% urban) return(0.40) if(geo %in% suburban) return(0.45) if(geo %in% rural) return(0.55) return(0.47) # default fallback}azones <- c("Fairfax County","Fairfax City","Falls Church","Albemarle","Wise","Lee")df <- expand.grid( Geo = azones, Year = c(2019,2045)) %>% rowwise() %>% mutate( base = assign_lttrk(Geo), LtTrkProp = ifelse(Year == 2019, base, base + 0.06) ) %>% select(Geo, Year, LtTrkProp)write.csv(df,"azone_lttrk_prop.csv",row.names = FALSE)

azone_hh_pop_by_age.html:
File 08_azone_hh_pop_by_age.csv

June 1, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-azone_hh_pop_by_age.csv) defines azone_hh_pop_by_age.csv as containing the total household population in each azone, divided into six age categories: 0–14, 15–19, 20–29, 30–54, 55–64, and 65 Plus. These age distributions are used in multiple modules, including household lifecycle assignment and travel demand modeling. For example, the data below suggest that Albemarle has 18,444 people (age 0 to 14) living in households in 2024, with that value expected to increase to 22,439 in year 2045.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changes in population age distribution influence travel behavior and transportation demand. Different age groups exhibit distinct travel patterns, vehicle ownership tendencies, and mode preferences. Younger populations may rely more on transit, walking, or shared mobility, while middle-aged populations may have higher vehicle ownership and commute-related travel. Older populations may travel less frequently but may have specific accessibility needs.

Another scenario is to simply look at growth—as transportation is a derived demand, more population could lead to more travel. When looking growth (or decline), one should consider four files: azone_hh_pop_by_age (this one), azone_gq_pop_by_age, bzone_dwelling_units, and bzone_employment.

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

The file was developed using Census data for base year population counts and Woods & Poole population forecasts for future projections. The total population in each city and county was grouped into six age categories consistent with VisionEval requirements.

Base Year

Base year (2024) population data were obtained from the U.S. Census Bureau Table S0101: Age and Sex. The census table includes detailed age categories, which were aggregated into the six VisionEval age groups. For example, multiple Census age brackets were summed to form the 0–14, 15–19, 20–29, 30–54, 55–64, and 65 Plus categories.

Forecast Year

The 2045 forecasts were obtained by multiplying the 2024 values by the ratio of 2024 and 2045 age group populations available from Woods & Poole (2024). For example, Woods & Poole (2024) shows that Accomack County’s population age 0 to 14 for year 2024 is 5,246 and this is forecast to drop slightly by year 2045 to 5,058. The Census table showed a population of 5,556 for year 2024. Thus, the 2045 forecast for persons age 0 to 14 is 5,357 when one uses the ratio of Woods & Poole 2024 and 2045 data sets to achieve a 2045 forecast.

Notes

In cases where Woods & Poole grouped multiple cities and counties together, the combined growth ratio was applied to each individual locality’s 2023 population values. For example, Woods & Poole groups Fairfax County, Fairfax City, and Falls Church City into a single unit. There are 133 independent cities and counties in Virginia, and Woods & Poole shows these as 105 areas.

At the statewide level, this file may slightly overestimate the number of people in households, since Table S0101 appears to include total population—that is, persons who are in non-institutionalized group quarters. For most (122) of Virginia’s 133 cities and counties, the group quarters population is estimated to be less than 5% of the total population. For the 11 cities and counties where this is not the case, users have the option of subtracting the group quarters population found in a different file (05_azone_gq_pop_by_age) from the values in this file (azone_hh_pop_by_age.csv). However, note that the group quarters file is itself an estimate (extrapolated from the 2020 decennial census), so such adjustments may not be productive unless there is a large percentage shown below and a scenario requires such a differentiation.

azone_hh_veh_mean_age.html:
Explanation of how to get data for 07_azone_hh_lttrk_prop

April 6, 2026

Definition

VisionEval explains that the definition for azone_hh_veh_mean_age.csv is that it contains three attributes: Geo, defined as the name or identifier of the Azone (typically the county or independent city); Year, defined as the scenario year; and AveVehAge, defined as the weighted average age of household vehicles in years. This parameter is a critical driver for the model’s vehicle engine and emissions modules, as it determines the rate at which older, less efficient internal combustion engines are retired and replaced by newer, potentially cleaner technologies.

In this implementation, the vehicle age is derived from household-level microdata to reflect the unique economic and demographic characteristics of each Virginia locality. Specifically, the data is sourced from the 2024 American Community Survey (ACS) Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS). This approach ensures that the model captures the real-world disparity between jurisdictions with high vehicle turnover and those with aging fleets. For example, the baseline vehicle age in Alexandria City is significantly younger (8.64 years) than in Charlottesville City (11.03 years), reflecting differences in local purchasing power and urban mobility patterns.

The average vehicle age serves as a proxy for the technological "health" of the fleet. While the baseline reflects observed 2021-2024 conditions, the target year (2045) incorporates projections of vehicle longevity and market trends. An example of the file structure and specific data points for Albemarle County, Charlottesville, and Alexandria City are integrated into the methodology below.

Methodology

The estimation of household vehicle mean age follows a structured computational methodology using R and the tidycensus package to process Census Bureau microdata. The process is designed to convert high-level PUMS data into granular, Azone-specific inputs for the 133 counties and cities in Virginia.

The methodology consists of four primary steps:

Data Acquisition and Cleaning: Using the get_pums function, household-level records for Virginia (State FIPS 51) are retrieved. The variable of interest is VEHAGE, which records the age of the most recent vehicle in the household. Records are filtered to exclude households with missing data or zero vehicles (VEHAGE > 0) to ensure the mean reflects the active household fleet.

Geographic Crosswalking: Because PUMS data is reported by Public Use Microdata Areas (PUMAs) rather than counties, a geographic crosswalk is applied. Each PUMA is mapped to its corresponding Virginia FIPS codes using an allocation factor (afact). This allows the model to correctly distribute vehicle data from broader census regions into specific Azones like Albemarle County.

Weighted Statistical Analysis: To produce a representative mean, a weighted average is calculated for each Azone. This uses the household weight (WGTP) multiplied by the allocation factor (afact). This step is vital to ensure that the sample accurately represents the total population of the locality. The formula used is:

Temporal Projection: The 2021 baseline is adjusted to 2024 and 2045 scenario years using a longitudinal aging trend. This accounts for the increasing mechanical lifespan of modern vehicles.

Albemarle County: Moves from 9.99 years (2024) to 10.74 years (2045).

Alexandria City: Moves from 8.64 years (2024) to 9.39 years (2045).

Charlottesville City: Moves from 11.03 years (2024) to 11.78 years (2045).

This automated R-based workflow ensures the process is transparent, replicable, and easily updated as new ACS data becomes available.

Note that in VisionEval as of April 2026, this file will cause an error if the number of years is greater 14.0 or greater. Values are therefore capped at 13.99 for compatibility.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval using this file is to evaluate how fleet stagnation or accelerated retirement programs influence long-term greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. Because newer vehicles are subject to stricter federal fuel economy standards and are more likely to be electrified, a scenario that successfully reduces the AveVehAge would result in a faster decline in regional carbon intensity.

For example, if a Virginia municipality implements a "Scrappage" incentive—providing rebates to residents who replace vehicles older than 15 years with new EVs—the modeler would decrease the AveVehAge for that specific Azone in the 2045 file. The model would then calculate the resulting shift in energy consumption. Conversely, if economic conditions lead to a "Fleet Stagnation" scenario where households maintain vehicles longer, the increase in average age (as seen in the Charlottesville projection of 11.78 years) would indicate a slower adoption of new technology, potentially offsetting the benefits of other transit improvements.

This file enables VisionEval to translate these demographic and economic trends into measurable transportation outcomes, allowing Virginia planners to see exactly how the age of the "rolling stock" on the road limits or enhances the state’s environmental goals.

Appendix

1.0 Steps performed:

1. Used the tidycensus package to download 2021 ACS PUMS household-level data for Virginia, filtering to records with non-missing vehicle age (VEHAGE). 2. Obtained a PUMA-to-county (Azone) crosswalk using a reliable source from the U.S. Census Bureau. 3. Merged the crosswalk with PUMS data and computed a weighted mean vehicle age using the person weights (WGTP) andd allocation factor (afact). 4. Aggregated results by Azone and exported a VisionEval-ready CSV file.

Resulting fields:

• Azone: County FIPS code for Virginia • AveVehAge: Weighted average vehicle age (rounded to 2 decimals)

Generated: Automatically using R and tidycensus, August 2025.

Step by step:

Data Source:

American Community Survey (ACS) 2021 Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS)

Survey: ACS 1-year PUMS

Geography: Virginia (State FIPS = 51)

Level: Household-level (housing unit records)

Variable of interest: VEHAGE = Age of vehicle (in years)

Weighting: Use WGTP (household weight) to account for sampling design

Step 3 – Load ACS 2021 PUMS Household Data for Virginia

r

CopyEdit

va_pums <- get_pums( variables = c("VEHAGE"), state = "VA", survey = "acs1", year = 2021, recode = TRUE, rep_weights = FALSE, household_variables = TRUE)

VEHAGE provides the age of the most recent vehicle.

Excludes person-level records: this is household-level data.

Step 4 – Clean and filter PUMS data

Remove households with missing or zero vehicles (VEHAGE == NA or 0):

r

CopyEdit

va_pums_clean <- va_pums %>% filter(!is.na(VEHAGE), VEHAGE > 0) %>% mutate(VEHAGE = as.numeric(VEHAGE), WGTP = as.numeric(WGTP))

Step 5 – Crosswalk from PUMA to County (Azone)

Since PUMS only provides PUMA codes and not county FIPS directly, we must join PUMA-to-county data. This can be downloaded from:

📎 Census Bureau Geography Crosswalks

For this step:

Download the "2010 PUMA to County Crosswalk" (or later if available)

Save it as "puma_county_crosswalk.csv" locally

Sample structure:

statepumacountyafact
5100101510590.65
5100101511070.35

r

CopyEdit

crosswalk <- read_csv("puma_county_crosswalk.csv") %>% filter(state == 51) %>% select(puma, county, afact)

Step 6 – Join PUMS to county-level crosswalk

r

CopyEdit

va_pums_joined <- va_pums_clean %>% left_join(crosswalk, by = "puma")

Step 7 – Calculate weighted average vehicle age per Azone

We now compute a weighted mean for each county using both:

WGTP = household sample weight

afact = allocation factor from PUMA-to-county crosswalk

r

CopyEdit

veh_age_by_county <- va_pums_joined %>% group_by(county) %>% summarise( AveVehAge = round(weighted.mean(VEHAGE, WGTP * afact, na.rm = TRUE), 2) ) %>% rename(Azone = county)

Step 8 – Export final VisionEval-ready CSV

r

CopyEdit

write_csv(veh_age_by_county, "azone_hh_veh_mean_age.csv")

azone_hh_veh_own_taxes.html:
File 11_azone_hh_veh_own_taxes.csv

March 10, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that the definition for azone_hh_veh_own_taxes.csv is that it has two attributes where VehOwnFlatRateFee is the “Annual flat rate tax per vehicle in dollars” and “VehOwnAdValoremTax” is the “Annual proportion of vehicle value paid in taxes.” Generally, it is presumed that in real (2024) dollars there will not be a change in either of these taxes.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changing the tax influences daily vehicle miles traveled and transit ridership. The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide is available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval further epxlains that because tehse “increase the cost of single occupancy vehicle travel” that one might explore “how increases in fuel taxes would impact the amount of vehicle miles traveled, the number of biking, walking, and transit trips, as well as CO2e emissions from single occupancy vehicles.”

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

The Azones reflect all 95 counties and 38 independent cities. The file combines two primary cost components: the annual flat DMV registration fee per vehicle and the vehicle property (ad valorem) tax rate for each locality. Base DMV registration fees for 2024 were sourced from the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and vary by vehicle type: $30.75 for passenger vehicles under 4,000 pounds, $35.75 for those between 4,001 and 6,500 pounds, $44.75 for pickups between 6,501 and 10,000 pounds, and $30.75 plus a $131.88 annual surcharge for electric vehicles. Because county-specific vehicle fleet mix data was unavailable, a statewide distribution based on FHWA/DMV trends was assumed: 80% passenger vehicles <=4,000 lb, 15% passenger vehicles 4,001-6,500 lb, 4% pickups, and 0.5% EVs.

Initial Calculations

Each Azone's flat-rate fee was calculated as a weighted average of these vehicle categories, with an additional $2 annual emissions surcharge added for localities in emissions inspection areas. The ad valorem tax rate data was taken from the Virginia Department of Taxation's Local Vehicle Tax Rate Table and converted from a rate expressed in dollars per $100 of assessed vehicle value into a decimal fraction (e.g., Fairfax County's $4.57 per $100 becomes 0.0457). Where local rates were not directly available, a default value of 0.0400 was used. To meet VisionEval's requirement for constant-dollar inputs, all monetary values were converted from 2024 dollars to 2015 dollars using the Consumer Price Index (CPI) from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, specifically 237.017 for 2015 and 307.026 for 2024, producing a conversion factor of approximately 0.772. These data are shown in 11_azone_hh_veh_own_taxes.csv.xlsx with a strikethrough.

Revised Calculations

After the initial file was developed, it was decided to use a 2024 rather than 2015 base year. Thus all tax amounts were multiplied by 1/0.772 to convert to 2024 dollars. Note that 2024 and 2045 amounts are all in 2024 dollars.

Other Notes

The resulting file contains one row per Azone for both the 2024 base year and the 2045 forecast year. The VehOwnFlatRateFee.2024 column holds the weighted, CPI-adjusted flat-rate registration fee, and the VehOwnAdValoremTax column holds the applicable property tax rate. This dataset enables VisionEval to estimate household vehicle ownership costs by multiplying the flat-rate fee by the number of household vehicles and applying the ad valorem rate to estimated vehicle values. Together, these values provide a key input for calculating transportation costs in Virginia transportation modeling scenarios.

Sources

- Virginia DMV - Vehicle Registration Fees: https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/vehicles#registration- Virginia DMV - Highway Use Fee for EVs: https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/vehicles/highway_use_fee- Virginia DMV - Emissions Inspection Program: https://www.dmv.virginia.gov/vehicles/emissions- Virginia Department of Taxation - Local Tax Rates: https://www.tax.virginia.gov/local-tax-rates- U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics - CPI Data: https://www.bls.gov/cpi/

azone_hhsize_targets.html:
File 12_azone_hhsize_targets.csv

April 10, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file contains information on non-group quarters households and provides household-specific targets for the population synthesizer. This file contains two attributes:

AveHhSize: Average household size for non-group quarters households

Prop1PerHh: Proportion of non-group quarters households having only one person

For example, the data below suggest that households in Albemarle County and Charlottesville City are growing in terms of size, with the average household size increasing slightly in Albemarle (and the proportion of one-person households therefore dropping), and more dramatically increasing in the City of Charlottesville. By contrast, the average household size in Alleghany County is dropping (and the proportion of one-person households is increasing.)

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changes in household size may affect travel demand. For example, one would expect different travel impacts from a set of 50 households with two persons per household than from a set of 100 households with one person per household. The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, explains that “While the base year populations often come from established data sources (e.g., Census) the future year population inputs can be modified to experiment with different assumptions about future population growth and demographic composition.”

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year

To obtain AveHhSize, Table B25010: Average Household Size of Occupied Housing Units by Tenure from the US Census Bureau was used. The base data is from 2023 and the total average household size was used. To obtain Prop1PerHh by Azone, Table S2501: Occupancy Characteristics from the US Census Bureau was used where again, the base data are from 2023. To calculate Prop1PerHh, this equation was used:

Prop1PerHh =

To convert these 2023 values to 2024, a short term trendline for the three years prior to the base data year (2020, 2021, and 2022) was developed, and Excel was used to calculate the slope of these data over the 4 years for each Azone, and added/subtracted that from the 2023 data. On average, this resulted in a small negative slope for AveHhSize and a small positive slope for Prop1PerHh.

Here is a snapshot of the intermediate file used to estimate the 2024 data for AveHhSize:

Forecast Year

The analyst has three different options for forecast year values.

One approach is to assume no change. Although household sizes have in some cases been decreasing since the 1970s, there is no guarantee this trend will continue. Similarly, in locations where household sizes have increased, there is not a guarantee this trend will continue. Thus, the local analyst may thus replace the 2045 values with 2024 values (presuming no change).

A second option is to presume that indeed this trend will continue. To make use of longer-term trends, data tables from the US Census Bureau were used for years 2019, 2016, 2013, and 2010, and then Excel was used to calculate the slope from 2010 to 2024, and this slope was initially used to predict the values for 2045 for each Azone going from 2019—that is, 26 years into the future to year 2045. However, this trend is likely unrealistic, as improbable values can result, such as values less than one, and sometimes negative, for average household size. A compromise was to add, for each Azone’s AveHhSize, the slope*15 to the 2019 value (rather than adding the slope*26 as done previously). This approach was used here.

A third option is to use Woods & Poole 2045 household size values for Azones and then to adjust the one-person households. This third option has not yet been pursued but may be considered later in 2026.

Appendix

Other Census data sources may be used. For example, the 2023 DP02 table from the census website as of June 2025 (DP02: Selected Social ... - Census Bureau Table) contains average household size for each city/county, while the Prop1PerHh column may be found by adding the male householder living alone estimates with the female householder living alone estimates and dividing that by the total households estimates to get the proportion of non-group quarters households having only one person. azone_payd_insurance_prop.html:
File 14_azone_payd_insurance_prop.csv

May 12, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that azone_payd_insurance_prop gives “the proportion of households having PAYD (pay-as-you-drive) insurance.” For example, according to the input file, the proportion of households who do not pay a flat fee for insurance but rather pay for it on per-mile basis is about 1%, for both the base year of 2024 and the forecast year of 2045, for Accomack, Albemarle, and Charlottesville.

The reason for this input is explained in the details of the Calculate Vehicle Ownership Cost module (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/verspm.html#verspm-calculatevehicleowncost). In sum, VisionEval estimates how much money a household can spend on travel and then limits daily vehicle miles traveled accordingly, and there are three characteristics that appear to the research team that can be used to more strongly associate costs with VMT—and thus reduce VMT if costs must be reduced to stay within the household budget. One of these is pay as you go insurance, in the sense that if you reduce VMT, you directly reduce insurance costs (compared to paying a set amount of insurance that is insensitive to VMT. Formally, this is described as “the cost of insurance is removed from ownership and shifted to marginal operating costs” in the Simplified Scenario Development Guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval.

(The other two attributes noted are workers participating in a cash-out program and the use of carsharing program, but those are not the subject of this input file).

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how increasing pay as you go insurance increases sensitivity to higher costs of DVMT. Logically, one would expect this file to be modified in conjunction with a file that influenced cost. For example, one could increase taxes using the input file azone_hh_veh_own_taxes and there would be some type of DVMT reduction. One could then see how shifting more drivers to a pay as you go insurance program along with the increase in taxes further influenced DVMT.

The document “Simplified Scenario Development Guide” gives a substantial amount of detail regarding this input file, suggesting that one scenario could be to see how not just DVMT changes (as more drivers adopt pay as you go insurance) but also an the “AvePaydInsCostPM” attribute which is the “average cost per mile for car insurance for those households which shifted” to pay as you go insurance (shown as “PAYD”).

Method Used for Virginia Statewide

Base Year (2024)

Unlike some states, Virginia allows pay as you drive insurance (see Table 1 of Guensler et al., Current State Regulatory Support for Pay-As-You-Drive Automobile Insurance Options, https://transportation.libguides.com/ld.php?content_id=63071776) so a nonzero proportion is feasible. Further, both the Simplified Scenario Development Guide and a 2022 update titled “Pay-As-You-Drive Auto Insurance: 2022 Update” (https://transportation.libguides.com/c.php?g=851090&p=8905167) suggest that improvements in technology will make pay as you drive insurance increasingly popular in the future.

That said, the research team could not find any information that gives an estimate of the proportion of Virginians who have pay-as-you-go insurance. One clue, however, is that this program would tend to be more appealing to Virginians who drive fewer miles than average. A surrogate for this estimate is the number of Virginians who participate in the mileage choice program, where in lieu of paying a highway use fee, Virginians pay a fee per mile (but this fee stops once a certain threshold is met). Thus the number of Virginians who enrolled in this program and who drove sufficiently low VMT so as not to meet this cap might be a good estimate for those who participate in a pay as you drive insurance program.

A review of Cummings (2023) suggests that this percentage might be estimated as:

There are 2 million Virginia vehicles that may a user fee

21,000 of these vehicles enrolled in the mileage based user fee program

88% of those enrollees did not meet the threshold (e.g., they saved money by participating)

This percentage is thus estimated as (88%)(21,000)/(2,000,000) or about 1%.

Forecast Year (2045)

This percentage may increase but the research team does not have any indication as to how this may increase. It appears more productive to presume that the percentage will not change for the baseline case and then include an increase in pay as you go insurance in conjunction with specific policies, such as an increase in fuel taxes. Thus the forecast year is left as 1%.

Reference

Cummings, S. Virginia’s Mileage Choice Program. Department of Motor Vehicles, Richmond, 2023. https://documents.ncsl.org/wwwncsl/Transportation/Scott%20Cummings%20Presentation%2012.2023_Jennifer%20Kraft.pdf. Accessed May 12, 2026.

azone_per_cap_inc.html:
File 15_azone_per_cap_inc

May 5, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that the definition for azone_per_cap_inc.csv is that it contains two attributes: HHIncomePC, defined as “average per capita household income,” and GQIncomePC, defined as “average per capita income for group quarters populations.” These values are specified by Azone and forecast year and are typically expressed in constant dollars (e.g., 2024 dollars). One element of potential confusion is whether the “HHIncomePC” is total household income or is per-capita income for persons who live in households. Examination of the documentation in another section (https://github.com/visioneval/VisionEval/blob/main/sources/modules/VESimHouseholds/inst/module_docs/PredictIncome.md) has led the research team to believe that the definition is the latter—that is, HHIncomePC is average annual per-capita income living in households, excluding group quarters, and GQIncomePC is average annual per-capita income of group quarters population.

For example, using 2024 dollars, the per-capita income for persons living in households in the City of Charlottesville is $36,807. In year 2045, this income is forecast to rise to $47,781 (in 2024 dollars). For persons living in military barracks or dormitories, this 2045 per-capita income is lower at $15,536 (again in 2024 dollars).

Possible Scenario

Imagine you are a planner for the Thomas Jefferson Planning District Commission (TJPDC). You want to know if the current expansion of Route 29 will be enough to handle traffic in 2045. One might consider four steps.

1. The Input: Income as a Trigger

The model reads your file and sees that Albemarle’s per capita income is jumping from $45,783 to $59,433—roughly a 30% increase in purchasing power.

2. The Behavioral Cascade

VisionEval doesn't just "add cars"; it simulates household choices based on that income:

Vehicle Ownership: In the model's logic, a household in a lower-density area like Albemarle with an income of almost $60K is statistically more likely to own three vehicles instead of two. The model updates the "Vehicle Availability" for thousands of simulated households in the county.

Value of Time (VOT): as per capita income rises, the model increases the “cost” of a person's time.

Result: A simulated commuter in 2045 Albemarle becomes less likely to take a bus (which has "waiting time" costs) and more likely to drive a personal vehicle, because their higher income makes them willing to pay for the "convenience" of driving.

Budgeting for Travel: VisionEval assumes households spend a relatively constant percentage of their income on travel. With more money, that "travel budget" grows. This results in more discretionary trips—more weekend trips to local vineyards or more shopping trips to Charlottesville—increasing the total Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT).

3. The Group Quarters (GQ) Factor

The model recognizes that the "Group Quarters" population (like students in dorms or residents in assisted living near Ivy) has a different travel profile.

Even though their income is relatively high, the model’s Land Use component knows they live in high-density GQ housing. It will predict they have lower vehicle ownership than a traditional household, but perhaps higher use of ride-hail services (like Uber/Lyft) because they have the disposable income but lacks a personal car.

4. The Output: Policy Decisions

When you run the model with your data, the Ouput could tell a specific story—here is an example:

Table 2. (To be replaced with real data from the multimodal module)

Metric2045 income does not grow from 20242045 income grows as forecast from 2024Impact
Daily VMTBaseline+22%Higher congestion on Route 29.
Mode Share5% Transit/Walk3% Transit/WalkWealth "outpaces" transit; people prefer cars.
CO2 EmissionsBaseline+15%Higher income = more driving = more emissions.

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year

Base year (2024) data were obtained from Table S1903 for each city and county in Virginia. A total of ten attributes from that table were used. One attribute gave the median income per household (C03_001). The remaining 9 attributes were used to estimate the household size, where households are defined as family or non-family households. Six attributes gave the number of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 person families (C01_024, C01_025, C01_026, C01_027, C01_028, C01_029), one attribute gave the number of non-family households (C01_034), and two attributes gave the number of female and male non-family households with just one person, respectively (C01_036 and C01_039). These were used to estimate the average household size with two assumptions: a value of 7 rather than 7+ was used for attribute C01_029, and a value of 2 was used for nonfamily households that do not consist of a single individual living alone. For example, as shown in Table 1, calculations for Accomack County suggest an estimated household size of 2.15 persons. Thus, the median household income for Accomack County ($58,993) divided by this average household size (2.15) yields a per-capita income for persons living in households (HHIncomePC.2024) in year 2024 dollars of $27,436.

Group quarters population was based on Census Table S2601A which provides information for the entire state of Virginia—not by Azone, where the attribute used was noninstitutionalized group quarters population (e.g., dormitories, military barracks but not jails nor skilled nursing facilities). Thus the same value was used for all Azones for 2024 which was $11,542.

Forecast Year

For per-capita incomes of persons who live in households, the 2045 income was forecast by multiplying the 2024 income by the ratio of 2024 and 2045 per-capita incomes available from Woods & Poole (2024). The manner in which Woods & Poole defines income may differ from that of the the U.S. Census Bureau, and thus the rate of change is used. For example, Woods & Poole (2024) forecasts that in year 2024 dollars, Accomack’s per-capita income will increase from $45,408 to $65,058 and thus a 43% increase is applied to the 2024 value from the U.S. Census Bureau ($27,246) to obtain a 2045 forecast value of $65,058.

For per-capita incomes of persons who live in group quarters, the 2024 value of $11,542 was increased by an average (by jurisdiction) increase of 34.6% to yield a 2045 value of $15,536.

Reference

azone_prop_sov_dvmt_diverted.html:
File 16_azone_prop_sov_dvmt_diverted.csv

June 4, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-azone_prop_sov_dvmt_diverted.csv) defines azone_prop_sov_dvmt_diverted.csv as containing one attribute: PropSovDvmtDiverted, defined as the “proportion of household daily vehicle miles traveled (DVMT) in single-occupant vehicle (SOV) tours with round-trip distances of 20 miles or less that are diverted to bicycling or other slow-speed modes of travel.” Changing this value represents a policy or scenario goal, rather than a directly observed quantity, and is specified by Azone and forecast year. For more about the details of how, exactly, this input file is used and how results may be interpreted, see the section under Other Notes.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to evaluate how investments in active transportation infrastructure, such as bike lanes, greenways, and pedestrian improvements affect short-distance travel behavior. As described in Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development, increasing the proportion of short SOV trips diverted to non-motorized modes can:

reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT)

lower greenhouse gas emissions

improve public health outcomes

reduce congestion for short trips

Because this variable applies specifically to short tours (≤20 miles round trip), it targets trips that are most realistically substitutable with biking or walking. For example, one might develop a scenario where in year 2045, the base condition is that there will be no change in this value—but then a scenario is that there will be a deliberate policy to favor active travel, such as significant investment in infrastructure, improved safety and accessibility for biking and walking, and cultural and behavioral shifts toward non-motorized travel. In that scenario, the proportion of PropSovDvmtDiverted could be increased from 2024 to 2045 as shown in bold in the figure below.

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

The Azones reflect all 95 counties and 38 independent cities in Virginia. This file specifies a scenario-based policy target for shifting short-distance SOV travel to active modes. Because detailed household travel survey data was not available for all Azones, this implementation uses a stylized, policy-driven approach, assigning low baseline values for the base year (2024) and the forecast year (2045). Then, in a scenario, users may choose more ambitious targets for year 2045.

Initial Calculations

Unlike other input files, PropSovDvmtDiverted is not directly estimated from observed data, but instead represents a scenario assumption reflecting policy goals and behavioral change potential. The team chose low baseline values of 0.01 for all counties and 0.02 for all cities. These values reflect limited existing active transportation mode share and higher baseline walking/biking rates in urban areas. Low values of this (for a baseline case) have been used elsewhere, notably in the RVMPO documentation case on Github (0.04 for 2010 and 0.08 for 2038) and for the Fresno area (roughly 0.01; see RSG, Inc. (2025).

Other Notes

Table 1 shows four runs for a small hypothetical scenario where no inputs were changed except the value of PropSovDvmtDiverted. In this particular run (based on the household output file with one row for each synthesized household), notice that the output attributes (obtained by summing all rows) for total walk trips, bike trips, and transit trips all increased but only very slightly as PropSovDvmtDiverted increased. When comparing the top and bottom rows, for example, it is clear that the change in vehicle trips taken by households (4,147) is much larger than the change in walk, bike, and transit trips (a total of 256). Thus increasing PropSovDvmtDiverted in this case is not assigning those trips to walk, bike, and transit trips but rather appears to be putting them somewhere else.

Table 1. Examples of VisionEval Runs with Different Values of Diversion
