aThese are person trips—that is, with PropSovDvmtDiverted = 0.0, a total of 28,571 transit passenger trips resulted. If every transit vehicle always had 10 people, then these 28,571 transit passenger trips would be 2,857 transit vehicle trips.

In the same output file is an output attribute for each synthesized household called SovDvmtProp; this attribute is the proportion of household DVMT in single vehicle occupant trips. For the case of PropSovDvmtDiverted = 0.0, multiplication of SovDvmtProp by the DVMT for each household gives a total of 28,592 DVMT, which is roughly the difference in DVMT between the top and bottom rows of Table 1.

Thus, increasing PropSovDvmtDiverted is leading more trips from other modes, but these are not reflected directly in walk, bike, and transit trips. Rather, they are reflected in other output attributes. One of these is the output attribute “PropDVMTDiverted.” For all households, this value is 0 for the case of PropSovDvmtDiverted=0.0 but is nonzero for all households (which have any values for the output attribute SovDvmtProp) when PropSovDvmtDiverted = 1. Another attribute is AveTrpLenDiverted which is defined as the “average length in miles of vehicle trips diverted to bicycling, electric bikes, or other 'low-speed' travel modes.” The sum of this attribute (when PropSovDvmtDiverted = 1) is 50,281—considerably higher than the DVMT differences between the top and bottom rows—the research team expected this difference to be smaller (e.g., 28,592 if all travel were conserved).

As shown above, the resulting file contains one row per Azone for both the base year and forecast year. These values are used by VisionEval to reduce SOV travel demand for short trips and reallocate those trips to active transportation modes. Because this variable represents a policy-sensitive parameter, it is particularly useful for testing the impacts of investments in:

bicycle infrastructure

pedestrian improvements

complete streets policies

In sum, higher values of PropSovDvmtDiverted will result in lower modeled VMT and increased non-motorized travel activity.

Replication Procedure

To recreate this file:

Define Azones

Assign baseline diversion rates (2024) based on current conditions

Assign future diversion targets (2045) based on policy assumptions

Ensure values are between 0 and 1

Export to CSV

Example R Script

library(dplyr)azones <- c("Albemarle County","Charlottesville City")years <- c(2024,2045)values <- c( 0.03, 0.25, # Albemarle 0.05, 0.35 # Charlottesville)df <- data.frame( Geo = rep(azones, each = 2), Year = rep(years, times = 2), PropSovDvmtDiverted = values)write.csv(df, "azone_prop_sov_dvmt_diverted.csv", row.names = FALSE)

How the Input File is Used in VisionEval

This input file is used directly by the VisionEval module DivertSovTravel (located in the VEHouseholdTravel package) and indirectly affects results in the downstream module ApplyDvmtReductions. Within the model workflow, DivertSovTravel is executed after household travel demand has been calculated (i.e., after CalculateHouseholdDvmt, CalculateAltModeTrips, and CalculateVehicleTrips), and before system performance calculations. This means the diversion specified in this file modifies already-estimated household travel behavior rather than influencing initial travel generation.

The key input variable, PropSovDvmtDiverted, is interpreted by the model as a target proportion of short-distance SOV travel (≤20 miles round trip) to be diverted, not as a direct reduction applied uniformly to all households.

The module applies this input in the following steps:

Identify Eligible Travel

For each household, the model estimates the portion of daily vehicle miles traveled (DVMT) that occurs in single-occupant vehicle (SOV) tours with round-trip distances of 20 miles or less (in Urban or Town location types). These trips represent the subset of travel most likely to be shifted to bicycling or other low-speed modes.

Calculate Azone-Level Diversion Target

For each Azone and model year, the total eligible SOV DVMT (from urban and town households only) is summed. This total is multiplied by PropSovDvmtDiverted to determine the total amount of eligible DVMT to be diverted in that Azone.

Allocate Diversion Across Households

The total diversion is distributed back to individual households based on:

the amount of eligible SOV DVMT they generate, and

the average length of their qualifying trips (shorter trips are more likely to be diverted).

This allocation is not uniform; households with more short SOV travel and shorter trips receive a larger share of the diversion.

Generate Household-Level Outputs

The module produces household-level values including:

the proportion of DVMT diverted (PropDvmtDiverted), and

the average trip length of diverted travel.

These outputs are then passed to the ApplyDvmtReductions module, which reduces household DVMT accordingly and reallocates diverted travel to non-motorized modes. Note, however, that as shown in Table 1, this reallocation may not be evident in the walk, bike, or transit trips—rather, one must look at the DVMTDiverted outputs as well.

An important limitation is that diversion is only applied to households in Urban and Town location types, reflecting the assumption that rural areas have limited feasibility for shifting SOV travel to biking or similar modes.

Interpretation of Input Values

Because this file defines a scenario target rather than an observed rate, the values should be interpreted as the share of eligible short-distance SOV travel that could realistically be shifted under a given policy scenario.

For example:

A value of 0.05 implies that 5% of eligible short SOV DVMT is diverted.

A value of 0.25 implies a much more aggressive scenario in which 25% of that eligible travel is shifted to active modes.

Importantly, these values do not mean that all households reduce their travel by that percentage. Instead, the diversion is distributed unevenly across households based on modeled travel characteristics, meaning that some households experience larger reductions than others. As a result, this parameter should be understood as controlling the Azone-level diversion target, rather than specifying a direct behavioral change for individual households.

azone_relative_employment.html:
File 17_azone_relative_employment.csv

April 15, 2026

Definition of the Input File

The meaning of the attributes in this file was surprising to the research team.

Interpretation 1

In its summary, VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file “contains ratio of workers to persons by age” which would lead one to suspect that the attributes should be less than 1.0 for all age groups and especially for young children. However, this is not the case. In a more detailed section, the documentation explains that this CSV file “contains the ratio of workers to persons by age cohort in the model year relative to the model estimation data year” (emphasis added).

For example, for the attribute “RelEmp15to19” the definition is “Ratio of workers to persons age 15 to 19 in model year versus in estimation data year.” In other words, suppose 30% of persons age 15 to 19 work in 2024. The proper value for this attribute is not 30%. Instead, one needs to ask “what proportion of persons age 15 to 19 in 2045 will work?” and then compare that proportion to the 2024 proportion. Thus if analysts believe that 30% of persons age 15 to 19 in 2024 work and that this ratio will be 30% in year 2045, then the ratio should be 30%/30% = 1.0. Indeed in the sample data associated with RVMPO, the values are 1.0 for all age groups.

Table 1. Explanation of Azone_Relative_Employment from the VisionEval Documentation

GeoYearRelEmp15to19RelEmp20to29RelEmp30to54RelEmp55to64RelEmp65Plus
RVMPO201011111
RVMPO203811111

Interpretation 2

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval suggests a different definition. The Guide states that this CSV file indicates “the proportion of persons in each age group who are in the labor force. For instance, the table suggests that in 2045, 90% of all persons aged 15 and above would be in the labor force.”

Table 3. Explanation of Azone_Relative_Employment from the Playbook

Choosing the Interpretation

Examination of another section of the VisionEval documentation, coupled with another sentence in A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, leads the research team to believe that materially the first interpretation should be used. The VisionEval documentation at VisionEval/sources/modules/VESimHouseholds/inst/module_docs/PredictWorkers.md at main · VisionEval/VisionEval · GitHub states the following where the preceding paragraph had indicated, for a particular household, that there was a 70% probability that a person age 20-29 was a worker:

If the user has supplied optional inputs for the ratio of employment for the age group in the forecast year relative to the year of the model estimation dataset, that input is multiplied by the estimated worker probability to determine the sampling probability. For example, if the year of the model estimation data is 2000 and the forecast year is 2010, and if the user specifies that the employment rate of 20-29 year olds in 2010 was 95% of the employment rate of that age group in 2000, then the worker probability in the example above (0.7) is multiplied by 0.95 to calculate the sampling probability. (emphasis added).

In other words, if the user thought that the ratio of workers to households would remain constant from the base year to the forecast year, then value in azone_relative_employment should be 1.00 rather than 0.95.

It is possible that A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval nonetheless supports the first interpretation. A final sentence is included therein, which states that this file “is intended to be an adjustment beyond the ACS PUMS data used to create the synthetic population.” In that sense, if the ACS PUMS data presumes a certain ratio of workers to persons in an age group, and the analyst believes this ratio will change, in a forecast year, then presumably a number other than 1.0 could be used.

However, to be clear, the numbers in this file do not indicate the actual ratio of workers to people—rather, they indicate how that ratio will change. As an example, Virginia data from the U.S. Census Bureau reported by the Office of Intermodal Planning and Investment that for year 2021, of the 1.096 million persons age 54-65 living in Virginia, about 736,000 of them are in the labor force, for a ratio of 67.1%. If it is assumed this ratio will not change—that is in 2045 it will be the case that 67.1% of persons in this age group are in the labor force—then the value of 1 is retained. This is the assumption for Charlottesville and Albemarle below.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changes in relative employment affect travel demand. For example, in year 2045 perhaps more or fewer seniors will be employed. One could use a value of 0.90 to say that fewer seniors will be working year 2045 and thus examine changes in DVMT.”

Method Used for Virginia

For the base case, a value of 1 was used for the base and forecast year.

Appendix

The research team used the percent of people in the labor force under the presumption that while unemployment may never be 0%, the labor force is an indication of people who will in some form be generating travel demand.

That said, in the example above, if one wanted to use persons employed rather than persons in the labor force, then the percentage would be 64.9% rather than 67.1%.

File 18_azone_veh_use_taxes.csv

March 23, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that the azone_veh_use_taxes file has three attributes—the fuel tax per gallon, a tax on vehicle-miles traveled, and “PevSurchgTaxProp” which is the proportion of the gas tax levied on plug-in electric vehicles. For example, suppose a gas-powered vehicle will pay $229.22 in fuel taxes over a year. A plug-in electric vehicle requires no fuel and thus “PevSurchgTaxProp” would be zero—except that in Virginia, all electric vehicles pay a fee of $131.88. Thus “PevSurchgTaxProp” is 131.88/229.22 or about 0.575. Generally, it is presumed that in real (2024) dollars there will not be a change in either of these taxes.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changing the tax influences daily vehicle miles traveled and use of other modes, especially with respect to impacts on electric vehicle travel and hence greenhouse gas emissions.

As is the case with another input (azone_hh_veh_own_taxes), the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide is available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval further explains that because these “increase the cost of single occupancy vehicle travel” that one might explore “how increases in fuel taxes would impact the amount of vehicle miles traveled, the number of biking, walking, and transit trips, as well as CO2e emissions from single occupancy vehicles.” For example, the guide notes that “Per mile fees that have been implemented by DOTs across the U.S. have been less than one dollar – typically between 1 and 3 cents.”

Method Used for Virginia Statewide

For the three attributes, data were estimated as follows:

Fuel tax. For the period July 1, 2024-June 30, 2025 Virginia fuel taxes were 30.8 cents per gallon (for gasoline) and 31.8 cents per gallon (for diesel) and have been reported by FHWA as 31 cents per gallon. The federal tax is 18.4 cents per gallon. Thus in 2024 dollars, the fuels tax per gallon is reported in VisionEval for 2024 as 31.0 cents (roughly for regular fuel or diesel) + 18.4 cents = 49.4 cents per gallon. This value is left the same for year 2024 and 2045 as both costs are in 2024 dollars. These are based on sources 1-4 below.

VMT tax. Virginia does not have a VMT tax so this value is zero.

PevSurchgTaxProp represents a surcharge on electric vehicles designed to capture this fuels tax. In 2025, the highway use fee for electric vehicles was $131.88 as shown in source 5. The base scenario assumes that the Virginia Department of Motor Vehicles will adjust the fee periodically adjust for inflation. For a gas vehicle that gets 25 miles per gallon and drives an average of 11,600 miles per year, that vehicle would spend 11,600 miles/25 gallons * tax of 49.4 cents per gallon = $229.22 per year. Thus, the electric vehicle pays $131.88/$229.22 = 0.575 of the gas tax cost.

Local planners may modify these values. For instance, if a region includes a supplemental tax for transportation, this would be added to the base (2024) year.

azone_vehicle_access_times.html:
Explanation of how to get data for 19_azone_vehicle_accss_times

April 6, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that the definition for azone_vehicle_access_times.csv is that it contains three attributes: OwnedVehAccessTime, defined as the average time required to access and egress from a household-owned vehicle; HighCarSvcAccessTime, defined as the average time required to access and egress from a high service level car service; and LowCarSvcAccessTime, defined as the average time required to access and egress from a low service level car service. All values are expressed in minutes and are specified by Azone and year.

In this implementation, car service access times reflect empirically derived estimates using observed ride-hailing data. Specifically, access times were developed using real-world wait time estimates obtained from Uber. Uber cities in Virginia | Uber .This approach ensures that the values used in the model more accurately represent actual service conditions across Virginia’s diverse geographic contexts.

Owned vehicle access time is defined as the time required for a household member to reach and begin using a privately owned vehicle, including any walking, preparation, or parking-related delays. While a default value is provided in this file, this parameter is inherently sensitive to local conditions and may be refined by individual jurisdictions. An example of the file can be seen below for Albemarle County, as well as Charlottesville and Alexandria City.

Methodology

The estimation of car service access times follows a structured observational methodology designed to capture both spatial and temporal variability in ride-hailing availability. For each city and county in Virginia, five representative locations were selected to reflect a range of land use and population conditions, including higher-density centers, typical residential areas, and lower-density peripheral zones. This ensured that the resulting values account for within-county variation in demand and service availability. For consistency, regullar economy Uber was used for both HighCarSvcAccessTime and LowCarSvcAccessTime data files.

At each of these five locations, wait times were collected at five distinct periods throughout the day over the course of a non-holiday 7-day week: morning peak, midday, evening peak, late evening, and overnight. These time periods were selected to reflect known fluctuations in travel demand and driver availability. Wait time estimates were obtained directly from the Uber platform, representing real-world conditions experienced by users. The resulting 25 observations per locality (5 locations × 5 time periods) were averaged to produce a single representative access time for both high and low service levels within each Azone. This can easily be adjusted for each municipalities needs.

High service levels reflect conditions where ride-hailing supply is relatively abundant and wait times are shorter, while low service levels represent periods or locations with reduced availability and longer wait times. This distinction allows the model to capture differences in service reliability and accessibility across varying conditions.

Owned vehicle access time was set to a default value of 5 minutes, consistent with VisionEval assumptions. However, this value is intentionally treated as adjustable. For example, in dense urban jurisdictions such as Arlington County, access times may be longer due to parking constraints, vertical residential structures, or increased walking distance to vehicles. Conversely, in rural areas, access times may be shorter due to immediate driveway access. As such, local municipalities are encouraged to refine this parameter based on observed conditions or local data sources.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval using this file is to evaluate how changes in the reliability and responsiveness of ride-hailing services influence household transportation decisions. Because access and wait time are key components of generalized travel cost, improvements in car service availability such as reduced wait times during peak periods can make shared mobility more competitive with privately owned vehicles. This may lead to reductions in vehicle ownership, lower vehicle miles traveled (VMT), and increased use of shared modes.

For example, if a locality implements policies that increase driver supply or improve service coverage such as designated pickup zones or partnerships with ride-hailing providers—the resulting decrease in access times could shift travel behavior away from single-occupancy vehicles. Conversely, in areas where wait times remain high, households may be less likely to rely on car service and more likely to maintain private vehicle ownership.

This file therefore enables VisionEval to capture the real-world operational performance of car service systems and translate those conditions into measurable impacts on travel behavior, mode choice, and long-term transportation outcomes.

bzone_carsvc_availability.html:
File 20_bzone_carsvc_availability

March 30, 2026

Definition

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that the definition for bzone_carsvc_availability.csv is that it contains one attribute: CarSvcLevel, which indicates the level of car service availability within each Bzone.

CarSvcLevel takes one of two values:

High – Car service (e.g., ride-hailing, taxi) is widely available and cost-competitive with private vehicle ownership, and therefore may influence household vehicle ownership decisions.

Low – Car service availability is limited or not cost-competitive, and therefore does not significantly influence household vehicle ownership.

This variable is specified by Bzone and year.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval using this file is to evaluate how the expansion of ride-hailing and shared mobility services affects vehicle ownership and travel behavior.

As described in Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development, increasing the number of areas classified as High car service availability can:

reduce household vehicle ownership

increase use of shared mobility services

reduce vehicle miles traveled (VMT)

shift travel toward more flexible, on-demand modes

Because this variable directly affects whether households consider car service a viable substitute for owning a vehicle, it plays a key role in modeling mobility transitions.

Methodology

Overview

Car service availability was assigned using a GIS-based classification approach grounded in measurable built environment characteristics. Specifically, Bzones were classified based on population density thresholds derived from U.S. Census data, which serve as a proxy for ride-hailing market viability.

Population density was calculated for each Bzone (persons per square mile), and the following thresholds were applied:

Urban (> 2,500 persons/sq mi): Assigned High CarSvcLevel

Suburban (1,000–2,500 persons/sq mi): Conditionally assigned

Rural (< 1,000 persons/sq mi): Assigned Low CarSvcLevel

To account for spatial spillover effects in ride-hailing markets, suburban Bzones located within 10 miles of an urban center were reassigned to High availability, other suburban areas were considered low, reflecting observed service coverage expansion beyond dense cores.

This approach is supported by transportation literature demonstrating that ride-hailing viability is strongly correlated with trip density, population concentration, and proximity to urban activity centers.

Initial Calculations

Car service availability was assigned based on the relationship between built environment characteristics and service feasibility, using the following logic:

Urban Bzones (higher density, mixed-use, shorter trip distances): → Assigned High availability

Suburban and rural Bzones (lower density, longer trips, lower demand): → Assigned Low availability

For the provided Bzones:

BzoneContextCarSvcLevel
515400002011Urban area near CharlottesvilleLow
517100051003Urban/central areaHigh
510030107011Suburban Albemarle CountyHigh

These assignments reflect the assumption that:

Areas with sufficient population and trip density support competitive car service markets

Areas with limited demand do not

Seen here, suburban bzone roadways are highlighted and marked surrounding Richmond center. Once within 10 miles, they become a central area.

Other Notes

The resulting file contains one row per Bzone for the specified year. These values are used by VisionEval to determine whether car service is considered a viable substitute for private vehicle ownership within each location.

Because this variable interacts directly with household vehicle ownership models, assigning High availability effectively enables substitution behavior, while Low availability disables it.

This classification is intentionally simplified to maintain:

transparency

reproducibility

consistency with other model assumptions

Replication Procedure

To recreate this file:

Identify Bzones within the study area

Classify each Bzone based on urban, suburban, or rural characteristics

Assign CarSvcLevel (High or Low) accordingly

Assign the relevant year

Export to CSV

Example R Script

library(dplyr)df <- data.frame( Geo = c("515400002011","517100051003","510030107011"), Year = c(2024,2024,2024), CarSvcLevel = c("Low","High","High"))write.csv(df, "bzone_carsvc_availability.csv", row.names = FALSE)

bzone_dwelling_units.html:
21_bzone_dwelling_units

April 24, 2026

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that the definition for bzone_dwelling_units.csv is that it contains three attributes: SFDU, defined as the number of single-family dwelling units; MFDU, defined as the number of multifamily dwelling units which have two or more units; and GQDU, defined as the number of non-institutionalized group quarters dwelling units such as dormitories and military barracks but not jails nor nursing homes. These values are shown below for four bzones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall), 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County, 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County), and 510030109041 (an area near the University of Virginia). Most bzones have no group quarters dwelling units.

Possible Scenario

One scenario in VisionEval using this file is to evaluate the impact of targeted housing policy and growth patterns in a specific area. For example, suppose the City of Charlottesville implements zoning reforms that encourage multifamily development near its downtown core and along transit corridors, while Albemarle County continues to experience primarily single-family suburban expansion. In this case, the model would reflect an increase in MFDU in Charlottesville and a higher share of SFDU in Albemarle. VisionEval would then simulate how these differing development patterns influence household behavior specifically, lower vehicle ownership rates and increased walking, biking, and transit use in Charlottesville, compared to higher car dependence and longer trip distances in Albemarle County.

This type of scenario is particularly relevant for real-world planning decisions, such as evaluating the transportation impacts of comprehensive plans or housing initiatives. For instance, increasing multifamily housing near employment centers or the University of Virginia could reduce short car trips and shift travel toward active modes, while also affecting parking demand and congestion. Similarly, areas with significant group quarters populations such as student housing or assisted living facilities—may exhibit lower vehicle ownership and distinct travel patterns compared to traditional households. By adjusting SFDU, MFDU, and GQDU across Bzones, VisionEval allows planners to directly test how land use decisions translate into measurable changes in VMT, emissions, and transportation system performance.

Note that when adjusting dwelling units, one must also adjust three population files (azone_hh_pop_by_age.csv, azone_gq_pop_by_age.csv, and azone_hhsize_targets.csv).

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year

Bzones represent small geographic units (generally Census block groups). This file estimates the number of dwelling units in each Bzone for both the base year (2024) and forecast year (2045).

The methodology follows a Census-based classification approach, using housing unit data and standard definitions of structure type. Where necessary, simplifying assumptions were applied to ensure full coverage and consistency across all Bzones.

Three Census tables were used.

One source is the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, specifically the “Units in Structure” table (Table B25024) for year 2024. This table provides counts of housing units by structure type, which can be directly mapped to VisionEval categories. Single-family dwelling units (SFDU) are defined as structures with one unit, while multifamily dwelling units (MFDU) include all structures with two or more units (e.g., duplexes, apartments, large multifamily buildings). (For two categories of housing, assignment to multifamily or single family was not clear. The research team assigned mobile homes to multifamily dwelling units given their closeness to each other but assigned “boat, RV, van, etc.” to single family dwelling units, thinking that these would tend to generate a larger number of trips comparable to single family dwelling units.

The second table was Table P5 from the 2020 decennial census. This table gives the population in group quarters dwelling units that are not institutionalized—that is, military barracks, dormitories, and others—but excluding skilled nursing facilities and prisons. The research team could not identify a group quarters table from the 2024 ACS.

The third table was Table B25024 for year 2020.

Then, the 2024 group quarters units were determined by multiplying the 2020 group quarters units by the ratio of 2024 single and multifamily dwelling units to the 2020 single and multifamily dwelling units. For example, for block group 510030106031, there were 363single family and 754 multifamily dwelling units in 2024, for a total of 1017 non-GQ dwelling units. The 2020 data showed a smaller number of non-GQ dwelling units (942) and 60 GQ dwelling units. Thus, the ratio of this change from 2024 to 2020 was applied to the 60 group quarters units in 2020 to estimate 71 group quarters dwelling units in 2024.

Forecast year

Data were acquired from Woods & Poole (2024) which give changes in total households for 2045 by Azone (city and county). The change from 2024 to 2025 for this value was applied to the 2024 data. (Note that in some cases, Woods & Poole aggregates a city and county; for example, Charlottesville City (FIPS code 51540) and Albemarle County (FIPS code 51003) are the same Woods & Poole are (51901).

For example, bzone 510030106031 is located in Albemarle County. Woods & Poole (2024) reports that the number of households in the combined area of Charlottesville and Albemarle County is forecast to grow from 66,064 in 2024 to 78,497 in 2045. This rate of increase (18.82%) was applied to the 2024 data to give the 2045 values shown below.

Reference

Woods & Poole, Inc. Technical Description of the Woods & Poole Economics, Inc. 2024 Regional Projections and Database, Washington, D.C., 2024.

Appendix—Other Notes

The resulting file contains one row per Bzone for each modeled year. These values are used by VisionEval to:

estimate household distribution

allocate population across housing types

model vehicle ownership and travel behavior

Because housing type is strongly correlated with travel demand, accurately representing the balance between single-family and multifamily units is critical for realistic model outputs.

Note for running VisionEval: if total SFDU + MFDU + GQDU is 0 for a given bzone, only SFDU is set to 1 to prevent crashing. Bzones are expected to have at least one usable dwelling unit.

Replication Procedure

To recreate this file:

Obtain Census housing data (units in structure) at the block group level

Classify units into SFDU (1-unit structures) and MFDU (2+ unit structures)

Obtain group quarters population data

Assign GQDU using a 1:1 population-to-unit assumption

Map all values to Bzones

Assign values for each modeled year

Export to CSV

Example R Script

library(dplyr)df <- data.frame( Geo = c("515400002011","510010902022","510010902023"), Year = c(2045,2045,2024), SFDU = c(307,1097,719), MFDU = c(449,148,134), GQDU = c(0,0,35))write.csv(df, "bzone_dwelling_units.csv", row.names = FALSE)

bzone_employment.html:
Explanation of how to get data for 22_bzone_employment.csv

March 10, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file has three types of employment--total, retail and service—where the cagtegories are based on EPA’s Smart Location Database. These values are shown below for three bzones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall) with large amounts of employment, 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County with some employment), and 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County). Not surprisingly employment is largest in the most urban zone.

Possible Scenario

Transportation is a derived demand, and generally two of those drivers are population and employment, such that all other things being equal, one would expect some type of change in employment to increase travel demand. However, as noted in the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, employment also is a land use factor in that land use is based on, in part, the degree of mix. Thus while one scenario is to see how an increase in employment without changing land use mix will increase VMT, emissions, congestion, and transit use, a second scenario is to see how redistribution of employment influences land use mix where in turn increases in the degree of land use mix could influence demand for pedestrian, bicycle, or transit travel.

Method Used for Virginia

Getting data for year 2022

Employment data were obtained from the Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics website which provides, at the block level, total jobs for year 2022 (U.S. Census Bureau, 2025). Because blocks use 15 characters (e.g., blocks “510010901011006” and “510010901011011”) whereas block groups use 12 characters (e.g., both of these are in block group 510010901011), the data could readily be processed in Excel such that the 3,793,766 Virginia jobs for year 2022 are organized by block group. For example, for block group 510010901012, the U.S. Census Bureau (2025) lists three blocks as shown in Table 1. Thus, the total jobs for block group 510010901012 is 115+1+3=119.

Potential Future Enhancements

There are two ways to improve this approach in future years.

The data that were used were purchased from Woods & Poole in 2024, as these had already been processed by VTRC. Woods & Poole updates these data annually, thus updated forecasts from year 2025 or 2026 could be purchased.

The multipliers given in Table 3 are based on total employment, which makes sense for the variable “TotEmp.” One could argue, of course, that service employment and retail employment in a given city or county are not forecast to increase at the same rate as total employment. Thus with additional processing, one could use individual two-digit NAICS codes to develop different multipliers for “RetEmp” and “SvcEmp.”

One reason for not pursuing the two bullets at this time is that for the 2024 data, VTRC purchased the right to share certain variables publicly from Woods & Poole—one of which was 2024 total employment. Thus the data used herein can be shared with others, in case questions arise.

Explanation of how to get data for 23_bzone_hh_inc_qrtl_prop.csv

April 6, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file has “the proportion of households in 1st, 2nd, 3rd, and 4th quartile of household income.” More specifically, these are proportions are intended to be by Azone (see https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-household-proportion-by-income-bzone_hh_inc_qrtl_prop.csv). For example, consider Bzone 515400010001 which is in the City of Charlottesville (Azone 540). The data below suggest that 28.8% of the households in this bzone are in the lowest quartile of income for the City of Charlottesville and that 15.8% of the households in this bzone are in the highest quartile of incomes for the City of Charlottesville).

Data for two other Bzones in a different Azone (003, Albemarle County) are also shown. For Bzone 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County with some employment), just 3% of these households are in the highest quartile of incomes for Albemarle County. By contrast, for Bzone 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County), 25.9% of the households are in the highest quartile of incomes for Albemarle County.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, does not give an explicit reason for modifying this input file. However, the VisionEval documentation (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-verspm-predicthousing) explains that these income quartiles “help VisionEval assign households to a compatible Bzone location.” Accordingly, one possible scenario is to examine how demand by Bzone changes due to uncertainty—e.g., one could assess, for instance, how changes in these quartiles for a given Bzone influence total model outputs, such as demand for transportation modes.

Method Used for Virginia

Users may wish to replace the statewide values used for Virginia with specific values. In theory, the quartiles should be tied to each Azone. In practice, the research team tied the quartiles to a statewide household income. The following approach was used:

Obtain Census data table B19001 for the five year dataset of 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024).

Find the number of households in the first, second, third, and fourth income household quartiles. For example, in Virginia, these are roughly as follows:

FROM $0 to TO half the households in the range of $45,000 to $49,999 (first quartile)

FROM half the households in the range of $45,000 to $49,999 TO three-quarters of the households in the range of $75,000 to $99,999.

FROM one-quarter of the households in the range of $75,000 TO $99,999 to two-thirds of the households in the range of $150,000 to $199,999.

FROM one-third of the households in the range of $150,000 to $199,999 TO infinite.

Convert these numbers to proportions for each Bzone and round them to three decimal places.

If the proportions sum to more or less than 1.000, then arbitrarily adjust the largest proportion by 0.001 such that the proportions sum to exactly 1.000.

For Bzones with no households, make the proportions each 0.250.

The calculations are in the file 23_bzone_hh_inc_qrtl_prop.xlsx with the data being in the file 23_bzone_hh_inc_qrtl_prop.csv

File bzone_network_design.csv

April 24, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file “contains values for D3bpo4, a measure for intersection density determined by the number of pedestrian-oriented intersections having four or more legs per square mile” which can be obtained from the Smart Location Database. These values are shown below for three bzones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall) with large amounts of employment, 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County with some employment), and 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County). Not surprisingly, the largest density of pedestrian-friendly intersections is in the most urban zone with the most rural bzone having the lowest value of 0.51.

For year 2045, values are presumed to be the same as for year 2024.

Possible Scenario

Urban design can influence travel behavior. As noted in the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, two related files—bzone_network_design.csv (this one) and bzone_urban-mixed-use_prop.csv can help one determine how walkable a given location is to other locations (e.g., New York City has values of 200-300). Further, one can see how changes in this value affect the number of walking trips (and with the multimodal module, the number of walking pedestrian miles traveled).

Method Used for Virginia

The EPA’s Smart Location Database (https://www.epa.gov/smartgrowth/smart-location-mapping#SLD) measures location efficiency using many characteristics including D3bpo4, which is an Urban Design (D3) variable. The data for D3bpo4 comes from 2018 HERE Maps NAVSTREETS, a road network database, as well as Census Block Groups as defined in the 2019 Census TIGER/Line databases, shown in the file EPA_SLD_Database_V3_2021. The values for D3bpo4 in Virginia bzones range from 0 to 450.448. Appendix A gives instructions for downloading these data if needed. There is one additional processing step which is also given in Appendix A, where the summarize within was used. An alternative that would be acceptable would be spatial join, but in this case summarize within may be more accurate.

Which Data to Download from the EPA Website: Download data for all areas with coverage

bzone_parking.html:
26_bzone_parking.csv

April 21, 2026

Definition of the Input File

This file contains seven attributes. Six are explained in the VisionEval Documentation. (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html). The first three refer to free parking spaces for residents of single family dwellings, multifamily dwellings, and group quarters residents.

The next three attributes refer to

the proportion of workers who pay for parking overall

the proportion of non-work trips that require payment for parking

the proportion of workers who pay for parking “in a cash-out-buy-back program”

The last attribute is the average daily cost for long-term parking—that is, if a tourist would pay $10 for parking for a single day but a commuter could purchase parking on a monthly basis for $100, then the commuter’s average daily cost would be $100/(20 work days in a month) = about $5.

For example, consider 3 bzones: 515400010001 (downtown Charlottesville), 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County), and 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County).

For all three bzones, the data suggest the number of fee parking spaces per single family dwelling unit is 2, per multifamily dwelling unit it is 1.2, and 0.1 for group quarters such as dormitories. In the most urban bzone, about 50% of workers pay for parking (compared to 15% for non-work trips), with most persons in a cash-out buy back program still choosing to pay for parking (70%). In that same urban zone, a monthly parker pays $6 per day. In the two less-urbanized zones, all parking is free and thus the last four attributes are all zero.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval devotes a substantial amount of attention to this topic, with the word “parking” appearing 60 times. Three scenarios suggested therein are: (1) examine how modes of travel change from auto to transit, bike, and walk as the parking pricing is raised; (2) determine if an increase in parking pricing in bzone X causes greater shopping to bzone Y with free parking, and (3) compare the imapct of work parking prices and shopping parking prices on global outputs such as VMT and emissions.

Method Used for Virginia

For the first three attributes, the same value was used for all Bzones in Virginia, where the number of free parking spaces for residents of single-family dwellings, multifamily dwellings, and group quarters residents was set at 2, 1.2, and 0.10. All three values may be adjusted by the analyst:

For single family detached dwelling units, the availability of street parking and driveways could influence this number in high density areas.

The free parking for multifamily dwellings should vary by location as a rough function of density, so this may be adjusted by the analyst.

For group quarters parking, using the example of college dormitories, the amount of free parking tends to be low, and the team selected a low percentage of 0.10. This value may be adjusted.

For the fourth and fifth attributes, the team indicated that for bzones with free parking, 0% of workers and 0% of non-work trips entailed payment for parking. For bzones with paid parking, the research team arbitrarily set the work trip percentage at 50%. This 50% may be adjusted, of course, with local information. Note the 5th attribute (PropNonWrkTripPay) is not given in the VisionEval documentation but rather described at https://github.com/gregorbj/OregonDOT-VisionEval/blob/master/documents/drafts/Non-Work_Parking_Mods.md?plain=1. If this attribute is excluded, then it is assumed that “non-work travel to a Bzone pays for parking if a parking cost has been assigned to a Bzone.” For bzones with paid parking, the research team set this to 15% to reflect that nonwork trips are more discretionary, but a different percentage could be chosen (although logically that percentage should be lower than that of PropWkrPay).

For the 6th attribute, the team indicated that 70% (most) of workers pay for parking in a cash-out-buy-back program for areas where there is a parking charge and 0% otherwise. The 70% may be adjusted in areas where information on travel demand management programs is available. If the TDM programs change behavior substantially, then presumably the 70% becomes a much lower number; if a TDM program has no impact whatsoever, then presumably the 70% becomes 100%.

For the last attribute—the average daily cost for long-term parking—the team hypothesized that this cost would have some relationship with a data element available from the Smart Location database: attribute D1D, which is the “gross activity density” (defined by EPA as the sum of employment plus households) on unprotected land. Gross activity densities for two areas in Northern Virginia—Ballston (left) and North Springfield (right) are shown in Figure 1. Then, monthly parking prices were obtained for these two areas from Spothero on April 21, 2026 for the month beginning May 1, 2026. For Ballston, a wide range of prices was chosen, but the research team selected the lowest one ($124) and for North Springfield, no parking was shown (which was to be expected as there is ample parking along the street free of charge).

Figure 1. Gross Activity Density for Ballston (left) and North Springfield (right)

A few other locations provided additional data points. These were Charlottesville (lowest monthly price of $120), Alexandria (lowest monthly price of $180), Tysons Corner (lowest monthly price of $90), Norfolk near Granby Street (lowest monthly price of $77), and Richmond (lowest monthly price of $123 near the state Capitol). Table 1 shows a rough view of these monthly prices, ranges of gross activity densities near these locations, and an estimated daily price based on dividing the monthly price by 20 working days and rounding to the nearest dollar.

Table 1. Sampled Monthly Parking Prices and Gross Activity Densities

LocationMonthly price (Daily price)Gross Activity Density

Table 1 is instructive: gross activity density is not the sole indicator of monthly parking price, which is not surprising given that the monthly prices shown were based on rough sampling and the fact that parking markets vary by location. The approach chosen by the team was as follows:

For areas with a density of 100 or more, the price was set to $9 per day. This was applicable for 30 bzones.

For areas ranging from a density of 15 to 99, the price was $9*(density/100) rounded to the nearest dollar. This was applicable for 400 bzones.

For areas where the gross activity density was 15 or below, the price was set to zero. This was applicable for 5533 bzones.

Not surprisingly, most of the state’s bzones (5533/5963 or 93%) offer free parking as shown in Figure 2.

Creation of Bzone_Transit_Service.csv

March 10, 2026

Definition of the Input File

Bzone_transit_service.csv is defined as the “aggregate frequency of transit service within 0.25 miles of block group boundary per hour during evening peak period” and is based on attribute D4c within the EPA Smart Location Database. This is one of two key transit inputs in VisionEval (see https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html).

These values are shown below for three bzones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall) with large amounts of employment, 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County with some employment), and 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County). Not surprisingly, one has greater transit service in the most urban area with the rural area having none.

For year 2045, values are presumed to be the same as for year 2024.

Possible Scenario

As noted in the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, two related files should be manipulated: bzone_transit_service.csv (this one) and marea_transit_service.csv (one that indicates supply). In sum, one can ask “How would travel behavior change if the availability of transit were double what it is today? This topic explores the question of increasing the overall supply of transit options to a region. Transit considers both the extent to which the service is available (coverage) and the frequency of that service.” The guidance notes that while this file shows availability at the bzone level, one should also modify marea_transit_service.csv which shows total transit supply—that is, change both in tandem.

Method Used for Virginia

Version 3 of the Smart Location database (updated in 2025) was obtained from the U.S. EPA (2025) and overlaid with the 5,963 block groups in Virginia and was treated as the 2024 base year. The 2045 forecast year presumes that there will be no change in transit service frequency. The documentation available with this data source from EPA clarifies that D4c is “expressed as service frequency per hour of service” where the peak period is 4 pm – 7 pm.

There was not a perfect alignment between the zones used EPA for Virginia (roughly 5,332) and the 5,963 block groups used in Virginia in 2024. For example, Figure 1 shows that a highlighted block group from 2024 for Virginia. In the EPA database, this block group is not evident by itself but rather is a part of the larger block group. Accordingly, GIS processing (in this case, a spatial join) used the mean value of EPA attribute D4c for the Virginia 2024 block groups for year 2024. In addition, because EPA uses a value of “-99999” for attributes which have no transit service, such values were set to a frequency of zero.

Figure 1. The smaller highlighted zone is in the VisionEval larger nonhlighlighted zone are

For year 2045, the same transit frequencies for year 2024 were presumed as a base case—e.g., not improvement or reduction in transit service frequency.

bzone_travel_demand_mgt.html:
Explanation of how to get data for 28_bzone_travel_demand_management.csv

April 6, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file has two attributes: EcoProp (which is the proportion of workers who participate in “strong employee commute options” programs and ImpProp (proportion of households who “participate in strong individualized marketing program.” For example, consider Bzones 515400010001 (in an urban area of Charlottesville), Bzone 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County with some employment), and Bzone 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County). The proportion of workers who participate in a strong employee commute options program is very small in all cases (less than 1%) and is zero for the rural area. For the proportion of households who participate in a marketing program to encourage nonauto modes, the proportion is still less than 1% and again zero for most rural zone.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, suggests that “Workplace programs include employee commute options (ECO) programs such as increased workplace bicycle parking, carpool and vanpool programs, or employer-subsidized transit passes. Individualized marketing (IM) programs are customized to traveler needs, such as the Portland Bureau of Transportation SmartTrips Program…Users may be interested in exploring how these programs in combination with other policies can impact driving, use of public or active transportation modes such as biking or walking, or car and vanpooling.”

Thus one may see how an increase in the proportion of employers who encourage alternative modes of transportation (e.g., increase EcoProp from 0% to 10%) may influence total VMT, walking trips, walking trip lengths, and walking person miles traveled.

Method Used for Virginia

Printed pages 63-66 of the VTRC report Feasibility of Adapting VisionEval for Scenario Planning, available at http://www.virginiadot.org/vtrc/main/online_reports/pdf/22-r21.pdf, show how a combination of a review of the literature and interviews with stakeholders can be used to define these attributes for a specific location. In sum, a nonzero value should not be assumed unless there is firm evidence of a solid program that encourages individuals to use non single occupant modes. Examples of such programs are financial assistance to purchase or rent a van for vanpooling (which would affect EcoProp), secure locker facilities for bicycling (also affects EcoProp), or direct in-person communications with residents to encourage non-auto use (which affects ImpProp).

The approach chosen here was to assume that both EcoProp and ImpProp are 0 unless there is a density of at least 4,000 people per square mile. (At the time the VTRC report was done, ImpProp was assumed to be 0 unless a bzone had this density, and this statewide dataset applies this logic to the EcoProp variable). Thus for the base year of 2024, the logic is:

If the density is at least 4,000 people per square mile, then EcoProp has a value of 0.003 and ImpProp has a value of 0.009.

If the density is less, than both EcoProp and ImpProp have values of zero.

Most of Virginia has a density lower than this amount as shown in yellow, with the red areas having a higher density than 4,000 people per square mile.

bzone_unprotected_area.html:
Bzone_Unprotected_Area.csv

May 20, 2026

Definition

This CSV file has three attributes (UrbanArea, TownArea, and RuralArea) which yield the total area of unprotected (developable) land in each block group, or Bzone, in Virginia, categorized as Urban, Town, or Rural. The units are in acres. These values are shown below for three bzones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall), 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County), and 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County). All acres not protected from development fall into the urban category for the first two zones. For the rural area, half the unprotected acres are categorized as town and the other half are categorized as rural.

For year 2045, values are presumed to be the same as for year 2024.

Possible Scenario

Changing the number of unprotected acres by itself does not have any corresponding scenario. However, as noted in the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, changes to two related files—bzone_network_design.csv and bzone_urban-mixed-use_prop.csv can help one do the following: if we make an area more walkable, how does that influence VMT by reducing driving trips and replacing them with walking trips? This file appears to be necessary for such a question because only urban and town areas, but not rural areas, can be defined as walkable. Thus, this file is an input required to execute the scenarios described in association with bzone_network_design.csv and bzone_urban-mixed-use prop.csv.

Method Used for Virginia

Three different steps are needed:

Determine the total amount of unprotected area for each Bzone

Determine whether each Bzone is urban, town, rural or some combination thereof

Combine the results from steps (1) and (2)

Steps 1 and 3 are straightforward, and step 2 requires judgment.

Determining the Total Amount of Unprotected Area

The Smart Location Database has a field called Ac_Unpr which is the “Total land area (acres) that is not protected from development (i.e., not a park, natural area or conservation area).” GIS processing (in this case, the Summarize Within Tool) was used to get a total amount of unprotected land for each Bzone. (Rather than a spatial join, the summarize within tool was used. The reason for this was to get the best estimate of the number of acres when accounting for the fact that block group boundaries between the EPA Smart Location Database and those used in Virginia may not align perfectly.) For example, that processing showed that bzone 510010901011 has 984.18 unprotected acres.

All of Virginia’s 5,963 Bzones had a total unprotected acres greater than zero with nine exceptions. These 9 Bzones appear to all be water-only. An example of such a Bzone is shown in Figure 1, which contains Bzone 510019902000.

Figure 1. A Water-Only Bzone where there are no acres unprotected from development.

Categorizing Bzones as Urban, Town, and Rural

In terms of how to classify areas within the Bzone as urban, rural, or town, the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide (A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval) states that “The classification of the urban, town, and rural is generally up to the user.” Indeed this appears to be the case, given two contradictory examples:

A bzone should be either only urban, only town, or only rural. The VisionEval documentation (e.g., https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) indicates that in the past, areas of 50,000 or more people were considered urban, areas of 2,500 - 50,000 people are town, and everything else is rural. Elsewhere in the same document, the guidance states that “One method is to define land in MPO boundaries to be metro, for urban areas smaller than MPOs, land inside their UGB is a town. Everything else is rural.” (emphasis in the original). To the extent that bzones align with census geographies, one would expect a bzone to thus be completely urban, completely town, or completely rural.

A bzone could be a mix of urban, town, or rural. A review of the input file associated with the Rogue Valley MPO (RVMPO, the default files given with VisionEval) showed a different approach. For the 210 bzones and based on the amount of unprotected area (e.g., available for development), 104 bzones were completely urban, 17 were completely rural, and 87 had some urban and some rural.

Overall, it is critical that this classification of rural, town, and urban (or metro) be consistent with another input 31_bzone_urban_town_dwelling_prop which also gives the proportion of dwelling units in urban and town areas (and by subtraction, the proportion in rural areas is implied).

Accordingly, an approach was chosen that sought to initially categorize areas as urban, town, or rural. A dataset was obtained from ESRI titled “Urban and Rural Population in the U.S. (2020 Census) - Overview” which had the percent of population that is urban in each block group. A spatial join was performed, and then based on examining areas in Charlottesville/Albemarle and Culpeper, bzones were categorized as follows:

Urban if the Bzone has at least 75% of its population as urban

Town if the Bzone has more than 0% of its population

Rural if 0% of the population is urban

3. Combine the results from steps (1) and (2)

The Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval offers, however, two additional factors that were not immediately apparent to the research team and which make one consider not making unprotected acres entirely rural.

One concerns the use of mixed-use neighborhoods, where the guidance notes that when VisionEval performs land use modeling, two key input files—intersection density and proportion of development in a mixed use area—only applies to urban or town areas. That would mean that if one designated a bzone as rural only, one would not be able to examine a policy related to having some of the bzone be mixed use in the future. Thus rather than designating unprotected areas for a bzone as rural only, one might want to have such unprotected acres be rural only at present and then in the future have those unprotected acres be partly rural and partly town. A simpler approach, however, might be to simply have the unprotected acres be partly rural and partly town, and then shift the proportion of development (using bzone_urban_town_dwelling_prop) between these.

The other concerns trip diversion, where the Playbook mentions that azone_prop_sov_dvmt_diverted.csv is applicable only to urban or town areas.

Accordingly, to provide flexibility, the approach that was used was for rural zones to designate half their unprotected areas as rural and other half of their unprotected areas as town. It may be appropriate to change these percentages in the future, but for now it appears one can thus use the attribute bzone_urban_town_dwelling_prop to then shift growth between rural areas and towns.

Sources

ESRI. Urban and Rural Population in the U.S. (2020 Census) – Overview. https://www.maps.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=0f98fc66a9fa4f94953718578cbd77a8. Accessed March 10, 2026.

Estimating Bzone_Urban-Mixed-Use_Prop.csv

March 4, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/conceptprimer.html#urban-mixed-use) explains that the definition for bzone_urban_mixed-use_prop.csv that it contains “the target proportion of households located in mixed-used neighborhoods.” In sum, a mixed-use development “is one that includes residential and non-residential land uses in close proximity to one another, allowing for pedestrian access to many desired goods and services.” This proportion is reflected in the attribute MixUseProp shown below in an excerpt of the file which shows these values for three zones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall), 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County) and 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County).

In this instance, the households living in mixed-use neighborhoods is highest for the suburban area (0.74) and lowest for the most urban area (0.49). Thus, as discussed herein, the user may wish to replace these values with local information as discussed in the pages that follow.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval based on this input file is to examine how changing the number of households that lived in mixed use areas influences daily vehicle miles traveled and greenhouse gas emissions. Such a scenario would entail changes to this file (Bzone_Urban-Mixed-Use_Prop.csv) as well as changes to a related input file, which is the walkability of the zone (bzone_network_design.csv).

Options for Choosing Inputs

Additional documentation suggests that there are two options for defining this target:

The user can “establish targets for the proportion of households in each Bzone that are located in urban mixed-use neighborhoods.” This option could be useful if the user wanted to evaluate an explicit planning policy that encouraged mixed use neighborhoods.

The user can enter the value “NA” and VisionEval will calculate this value for you. (The link for this more detailed documentation is https://github.com/VisionEval/VisionEval/blob/main/api/VE_Training_March_13-14_2019/VE_Training.md#45-calculateurbanmixmeasure-module)

General Methods for Estimation

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide (available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval) explains that to obtain these Bzone values “a user should draw upon local land use data that reflects the areas that are considered mixed use within their jurisdiction….The ratios can be approximated by numbers of jobs to workers or ratios of employment to housing, depending on the available data.” Such data may be available in more than one location. For instance, localities may have employment data by Bzone, and certainly population data are available by Bzone. The EPA Smart Location Database also has these data.

The aforementioned Task 7.2 document cites three variables that may be useful for estimating the number of households that are in mixed use areas two of which appeared productive in Virginia: D2A_JPHH (jobs/households) and D2A_EPHHM (an “entropy measure calculated from the number of jobs by sector and number of households” and which ranges from 0 for no mix to 1.0 for complete mix.) These numbers are rough proxies but not exact: that is, in areas with higher degree of mix, one would expect D2A_EPHHM to be higher. Examination of a few locations in Virginia with which the team was familiar showed that, for example, rural areas (Figure 1) tended to have lower values of D2A_EPHHM and D2A_JPHH than more urban areas which have a higher degree of mix (Figure 2).

However, this relationship is not exact. For example, the research team knows that the mix of land uses in the most southwest block group in Figure 2 is fairly uniform; in this suburban area, one would expect low values for entropy (yet 0.84) is shown. For that reason, users may replace the values used herein with local estimates of land use mix if desired.

Figure 1. Rural Area with More Homogeneous Land Uses

Figure 2. Urban Area with More Mixed Land Uses

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year Values

For the base year (2024) estimates of land use mix, the research team used the entropy as a starting point but chose the smallest value of these two quantities:

Entropy (e.g., D2A_EPHHM) which is always between 0 and 1

Entropy multiplied by Jobs per household (e.g., D2A_EPHHM* D2A_JPHH)

The intended impact of this was to use the entropy measure as an upper bound on land use mix but, in locations where entropy was high and number of jobs per household was low to reduce the land use mix accordingly. Thus a spatial join was performed such that the mean values for D2A_EPHHM and D2A_JPHH for each of Virginia’s 5,963 block groups were determined, and then the urban land use mix was calculated.

For example, consider block group 510030110004 in Albemarle County

Entropy = 0.74

Jobs/Household = 0.92

Mixed use proportion is thus 0.74*0.92 = 0.68 because this is smaller than entropy alone.

By contrast, consider block group 515400010001 in downtown Charlottesville.

Entropy = 0.49

Jobs/Household = 1.43

Mixed use proportion is thus 0.49 because this is smaller than entropy*jobs/household

Forecast Year (2045) Values

For the forecast year (2045) estimates, the 2045 mixed-use proportions were held constant at 2024 levels—that is, no changes from 2024 to 2045 are in the files. There are two reasons for this:

First, the region may wish to have a formal policy target for mixed-use development. Thus, the 2045 values shown in this file indicate that the proportion of each Bzone that is pedestrian friendly will not change. If a locality wishes to increase these proportions—e.g., formally decide to have more walkable neighborhoods—then the way to evaluate this policy is to have a new scenario with higher proportions of MixUseProp than those shown in the bzone_urban_mixed-use_prop.csv file.

Second, there is uncertainty in long-term urban growth patterns. Population growth varies by region, and applying a uniform increase across all zones could misrepresent local conditions. It is more appropriate to adjust values based on region-specific forecasts. To be clear, Virginia’s population is estimated to reach approximately 10.15 million by 2045, based on linear interpolation between Weldon Cooper Center’s 2040 and 2050 projections, which is a 17.6% increase from 2020. However, this does not necessarily mean MixUseProp will increase: while McKenzie (2023) projects continued urban growth, Lombard (2023) highlights rising move-out rates from cities toward exurbs.

Processing Files Used for Virginia

The Excel file Bzone_Urban-Mixed-Use_Prop.xslx has, for each Bzone, the GeoID, D2A_JPHH (jobs/households), D2A_EPHHM (the entropy measure labeled as “employment and household entropy”, the “mixed use proportion” all for 2024 data, and three additional attributes not used in these calculations but which localities may choose to adopt:

Attribute D2A_WRKEMP (the ratio of workers living in the zone to jobs located in the zone, labeled as “household workers per job”

Attribute D1A, which is “Gross residential density (HU/acre) on unprotected land”, and

Attribute D1D, which is “Gross activity density (employment + HUs) on unprotected land”

The Excel file Bzone_Urban-Mixed-Use_Prop.csv has just the GEOID and the mixed use proportion, where 2024 and 2045 values are identical.

Sources

McKenzie, B. Metro Areas Will Grow Larger, Rural Areas Will Grow Older. UVA Today, September 11, 2023.

https://news.virginia.edu/content/metro-areas-will-grow-larger-rural-areas-will-grow-older. Accessed February 22, 2026.

University of Virginia Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service. Virginia Population Estimates, 2024. https://coopercenter.org/virginia-population-estimates. Accessed February 22, 2026.

Lombard, H. After a decade of slow growth, many of Virginia’s exurbs are booming again. January 30, 2023.

https://www.coopercenter.org/research/after-decade-slow-growth-many-virginias-exurbs-are-booming-again. Accessed February 22, 2026.

bzone_urban-town_du_proportions.html:
Estimating 31_bzone_urban-town_du_proportions

March 11, 2025

Definition

This CSV file has six attributes all pertaining to where dwelling units are in terms of the urban, rural, or town portion of each bzone where SFDU indicates single family dwelling units, MFDU denotes multifamily dwelling units, and GQDU denotes group quarters (e.g., dorms). The categories of urban, town, and rural are up to the user (see discussion for data element 29_bzone_unprotected_area) but generally are based on census categories, such that some bzones are completely urban, completely town, or a mix of town and rural.

These values are shown below for three bzones: 515400010001 (an urban area near Charlottesville’s downtown pedestrian mall), 510030107021 (a suburban area near Route 29 in Albemarle County), and 510030110004 (a rural residential area in Albemarle County). For the urban and suburban areas, all dwelling units are in the urban area and none are in the area categorized as town. For the rural bzone, 30% of the single family dwelling units are in the town portion (with 70% in the rural portion), and all of the multifamily and group quarters dwelling units are in the town portion.

For year 2045, values are presumed to be the same as for year 2024.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, indicates that “growth allocation…allows the user to allocate different proportions of single family/multi-family/and group quarter housing units to the urban or town areas of a region” with the same document suggesting that for different allocation methods (e.g., growth from 2024-2045 perhaps is all in a rural portion of a zone or is all in an urban portion of a zone), one might be interested in the following outputs from VisionEval: total VMT, VMT per household, greenhouse gas emissions, fuel consumption, and walk trips and bike trips.

Method Used for Virginia

The approach used here followed that shown in 29_bzone_unprotected_area, where the bzone classifications were obtained. Generally bzones were all urban, all town, or a mix of town and rural. Then, for bzones that were all urban or all town, 100% of the dwelling units were placed in urban or town. For bzones that had a mix of rural and town, the research team did the following:

Place 30% of all single family dwelling units in the town portion

Place 100% of all multifamily dwelling units and group quarters dwelling units in the town portion.

Notes for internal use

See the description for data element 29_bzone_unprotected_area—that’s why this is so short.

marea_base_year_dvmt.html:
File 32_marea_base_year_dvmt.csv

April 15, 2026

Definition of the Input File

This is an optional file. VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file contains the base-year DVMT (Daily Vehicle Miles Traveled). If the user wants to use the default values, the data should be set to NA. Otherwise, the user can enter specific values. This file contains two attributes:

UrbanLdvDvmt: Average daily vehicle miles of travel on roadways in the urbanized portion of the Marea by light-duty vehicles during the base year

UrbanHvyTrkDvmt: Average daily vehicle miles of travel on roadways in the urbanized portion of the Marea by heavy trucks during the base year

For example, the data below suggest that base-year DVMT for light-duty vehicles and heavy trucks in Albemarle County is greater than that in the City of Charlottesville. Additionally, DVMT for light-duty vehicles is much greater than that for heavy trucks in both geographies.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, does not explicitly reference this file. In general one would expect changes in DVMT to yield changes in congestion, travel speeds, energy use, and emissions. However, VisionEval does not start with DVMT—rather, it starts with the drivers of travel demand (e.g., population, employment, and so forth) and then uses thse to obtain DVMT.

However, it is possible to use marea_base_year_dvmt for another reason—to understand the sensitivity of the results. For example, suppose a user wanted to evaluate how an increase in population and the number of households could increase total fuel consumption. A user would normally generate two model runs, where one might let marea_base_year_dvmt simply have “NA” values.

Model run with base 2045 values for azone_hh_pop_by_age and bzone_dwelling_units

Model run where the above two files were changed by 10% (or some other value)

From these two runs, the user could examine the change in DVMT and emissions. For example, one might find that DVMT increases by 12%.

The user might then do two more runs identical to those bulleted above but where marea_base_year_dvmt has not “NA” but rather the values given in this file. One could then see how changing assumptions about what your base year DVMT is changes the “12%” noted above. In this way, adjustments to marea_base_year_dvmt allow one to determine a confidence interval, of sorts, for certain scenarios.

Method Used for Virginia

To be clear, the user can elect to simply put “NA” in the lieu of the numbers shown such that one uses a file such as that shown below.

marea_congestion_charges.html:
Optional File 33_marea_congestion_charges.csv

April 15, 2026

Definition of the Input File

This is an optional file. VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file contains congestion charges by road type and congestion level. This input file is optional, so if the user wants to use the default values, the data should be set to 0. Otherwise, the user can enter specific values. This file contains ten attributes. The first five pertain to freeways: the dollar cost per mile of vehicle travel during periods of no, moderate, heavy, severe, and extreme congestion. The next five pertain to arterials and are the dollar cost per mile of vehicle travel during periods of no, moderate, heavy, severe, and extreme congestion.

For example, the data below suggest that congestion charges by road type and congestion level in Albemarle County are zero. If a county or city has its own congestion charges, the values can be adjusted at the analyst’s discretion.

Additionally, the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, explains that congestion charges must be entered as $/VMT, so real-world tolls need to be converted into per-mile values. Since the model has no network, users estimate the share of VMT affected by tolls and caulate an equivalent average charge by converting total toll revenue over the VMT subject to the toll.

Possible Scenario

One possible scenario in VisionEval using this input file is to see how changes in congestion charges affect key results such as congestion, travel speeds, and emissions. For example, a user can compare a case where a certain county has its own congestion charges with one where without it. In general, higher congestion charges leads to less delay, less congestion, higher speeds, and lower energy use and emissions. By adjusting the congestion charges, users can see how different starting conditions affect the overall results of the model. However, after several test runs, the team did not see a difference in results when congestion charges are applied.

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year, Forecast Year

All values were set to 0, as no reliable sources were identified. These values should be determined reflecting geographical characteristics.

Appendix

The marea_congestion_charges input file in the Sayed model uses the field name Congestion Charge Variables (e.g. FwyNoneCongChg.2010). To verify whether the year in the field name can be updated to the base year (2024), the Initialize module was reviewed. According to the VisionEval GitHub documentation (https://github.com/VisionEval/VisionEval/blob/main/sources/modules/VETravelPerformance/inst/module_docs/Initialize.md), the field name is flexible and can be aligned with the base year. Therefore, the original field name (FwyNoneCongChg.2010) was revised to FwyNoneCongChg.2024 to reflect the base year.
