Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html), in the example portion, explains that this optional file gives nine attributes, all of which refer to the “urbanized portion” of the Marea. (There appears to be a slight typo in the documentation but the example gives nine rather than eight attributes). Three attributes are for light duty vehicles—the proportion of VMT on freeways, arterials, and other roadways. Three attributes are for heavy trucks—proportion of VMT on freeways, arterials, or other roads. The last three attributes are for buses—the proportion of bus VMT on freeways, arterials, or other roads.

For example, in Charlottesville, 1.3% of all passenger traffic from light duty vehicles is on interstates or freeways—but this percentage increases to 7.5% for heavy trucks, which makes sense given that the latter tends to have a greater number of through movements.

Note that unlike Azones or Bzones, there should be just a single Marea file when running VisionEval. For instance, consider the Charlottesville-Albemarle MPO. There will be just one Marea file. A simple way to combine these files is just to average them. Alternatively, one can use the total VMT shown in for Albemarle County (about 3.38 M) divided by the total VMT for Charlottesville City (about 0.51 M) to weight the Albemarle percentages by about a factor of 6. These total VMTs are available from the Virginia Open Data Portal cited below but are also in the corresponding .xlsx file with this data set.

marea_lane_miles.html:
35_marea_lane_miles.csv

May 27, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file contains the number of freeway lane miles and arterial lane miles. In this dataset, these are shown at the Azone (city or county) level which the user may then combine into a single m_area. VisionEval explains that these are based on functional classification: roads will be classified as freeways/expressways, arterials, or some other source. (The VisionEval definition is at https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html#verspm-marea_lane_miles.csv.)

For example, in the table below, Albemarle County has 124.8 freeway lane miles and 384.3 arterial lane miles, both for the base year and the forecast year.

Note that unlike Azones or Bzones, there should be just a single Marea file when running VisionEval. In this particular case, it is appropriate to add the lane miles values.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval mentions this input file in response to the following question: “Available transportation supply dictates what transportation options consumers will use when traveling. Inputs in VE supply modules answer the following: How do changes in freeway and arterial lane miles affect DVMT?” For this reason, a scenario may be developed that changes these lane miles from the base case.

There are at least two considerations when using this input to develop a scenario.

One should consider what the 2045 base case should be. For instance, the input files herein used a base case of no construction, but perhaps a base case could be an increase in lane miles of some percentage (1%, 10%) or based on some forecast for future construction.

As discussed in the methods section, for cities there may be some error in the base case estimates of lane miles. Thus individuals can replace these numbers with their own estimates.

Method Used for Virginia

Three main steps were used to estimate the lane miles for each city and county. Note that the assumption in step 3.5 will affect the quality of the results. As a check, the research team obtained a shapefile of roads for the City of Charlottesville (https://opendata.charlottesville.org/datasets/charlottesville::road-area/explore?location=38.032270%2C-78.459289%2C13&showTable=true) and computed the area of these roads (29.5 million square feet) and converted these to lane miles assuming 12-foot lanes (466 lane-miles). This 466 lane-miles would be all roads—not just interstates and arterials but secondary or urban roads that should not included in 35_marea_lane_miles.csv. The method used below for Virginia gives, for freeways and arterials, about 147 lane miles for Charlottesville. These calculations do not guarantee that the figure of 147 is accurate, but at least the figure seems reasonable in that it is of the right order of magnitude and smaller than the total lane miles for all Charlottesville roads.

Optional 36_marea_operations_deployment.csv

May 26, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this optional file is used to specify the proportion of DVMT affected by operations for different road classes. The file is used in the Initialize (VETravelPerformance) and CalculateRoadPerformance modules. The file has six attributes which specify the proportion of freeway DVMT affected by ramp meeting or incident management, the proportion of arterial DVMT affected by signal coordination or access management, and the proportion of freeway or arterial DVMT affected by other “user-defined … operations measures.” For example, the table below suggests that for Albemarle and Charlottesville, there is no ramp metering, about half the DVMT (on interstates) is affected by incident management, about half the DVMT (on arterials) is affected by signal coordination for 2024 and 2045. Between 2024 and 2045, however, the DMVT affected by access management is forecast to increase from 10% to 20%.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval clarifies that three files may be used in to quantify “changes in policy and physical interventions to improve congestion through improved speed management and reduced delays.” This particular file can thus help one evaluate scenarios such as using signal coordination to improve traffic flow (and logically one could compare such operations experiences with the results from a capacity expansion that results from, say adding lane miles. The other two files that relate to operations are marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive.csv and other_ops_effectiveness.csv.

Method Used for Virginia

Three main steps were used to develop these values, with 2024 and 2045 values being identical except, as noted in step 3.4.5, the proportion of the statewide network subject to access management is believed to be 10% in 2024 and 20% in 2045. As is the case with all input values, the user can adjust these assumptions.

How the Data Were Processed

RampMeterDeployProp

According to the 2023 Freeway Management Deployment Data (XLSX), only District 9 reported having implemented ramp metering. However, the survey does not provide the number of ramps deployed. Therefore, a 5% deployment rate was assumed for counties/cities in District 9 (Counties: Arlington, Fairfax, Loudoun, Prince William / Cities: Alexandria, Fairfax, Falls Church, Manassas, Manassas Park), reflecting a limited implementation. The target year values were set equal to the base year due to the lack of public data on future deployment plans. These values may be revised at the analyst’s discretion based on regional characteristics.

IncidentMgtDeployProp

According to the 2023 Freeway Management Deployment Data (XLSX) and 2023 Arterial Management Deployment Data (State DOT District) (XLSX), all districts reported the use of incident detection and verification methods on both freeways and arterials. However, the survey does not specify the extent of deployment. Therefore, a 50% deployment rate was assumed for all counties and cities. This rate is consistent with the Sayed model and appears to be a reasonable assumption in the absence of more detailed data. The target year values were set equal to the base year due to the lack of public data on future plans. These values may be revised at the analyst’s discretion based on regional characteristics.

SignalCoordDeployProp

No public data sources are available; therefore, a 50% deployment rate was assumed for all counties and cities. This rate is consistent with the Sayed model and appears to be a reasonable assumption in the absence of more detailed data. The target year values were set equal to the base year due to the lack of public data on future plans. These values may be revised at the analyst’s discretion based on regional characteristics.

AccessMgtDeployProp

Access management regulations were formally adopted by VDOT in 2008 (amended in 2011) through the Virginia Administrative Code (24VAC30-73) and the Road Design Manual (Appendix F). These regulations mandate entrance spacing, intersection spacing, and median opening standards for new and redeveloped roadway projects. However, because the vast majority of arterial corridors were constructed prior to 2008, only a limited portion of the network has been retrofitted to meet the new standards. As a result, it is reasonable to assume that approximately 10 percent of arterial roadway mileage is subject to access management practices in the 2024 base year. Looking ahead, as more corridors are reconstructed or upgraded under VDOT’s long-range plans, the share of arterials with access management is expected to expand gradually. Therefore, for the 2045 target year, this analysis assumes the proportion will approximately double to 20 percent of the statewide arterial network.

OtherFwyOpsDeployProp, OtherArtOpsDeployProp

No public data sources are available; therefore, a 0% deployment rate was assumed for all counties and cities. This rate is consistent with the Sayed model. The target year values were set equal to the base year due to the lack of public data on future plans. These values may be revised at the analyst’s discretion based on regional characteristics.

Final Result

marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive.html:
37_ marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive.csv

May 26, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file tells one the extent to which there is speed smoothing.

For the first two attributes (FwySmooth and ArtSmooth) this number ranges from 0 (no deployment) to 1 (full deployment) of a system, such as a variable speed limit system or some other type of system, to manage traffic flow. (This presumably does not cover ramp metering which is part of a different input file (marea_operations_deployment.csv). As pointed out in the later Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, connected vehicle deployments may affect this value as well, although that document notes connected vehicles may be included a third input file (other_ops_effectiveness.csv)

The next two attributes are based on “policies with individuals committed to driving less aggressively with fewer harder braking or fast acceleration activities” where the 0 means percentage of drivers who agree to “drive in this manner” for freeways and arterials.

For example, the table below suggests that 10% of freeways in the City of Fredericksburg have a deployment of a speed smoothing system.

Possible Scenario

The aforementioned document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval mentions this input file as one of three one can use to “evaluate changes in policy and physical interventions to improve congestion through improved speed management and reduced delays.” (The other two input files are marea_operations_deployment.csv and other_ops_effectiveness.csv). Thus, presumably a scenario could be to evaluate how deployment of adaptive speed limit systems reduces fuel consumption compared to, say, a reduction in the number of trips or possibly an increase in lane-miles (if they latter reduces idling).

Method Used for Virginia

For the first two attributes, the research team identified one news article that discusses implementation of variable speed limits in Caroline, Spotsylvania, and Fredericksburg. That article is https://improve95.vdot.virginia.gov/variable/ and is titled “I-95 North variable speed limits.” The figure of 0.10 was chosen to indicate that a nonzero portion of freeways have a variable speed limit. Otherwise, however, the research team is not aware of firm evidence showing freeway and arterial smoothing in Virginia.

For the second two attributes, the research team could not find evidence of Virginia drivers practicing ecodriving. This practice certainly is possible; for example, a VTTI study, cited at https://www.claimsjournal.com/news/national/2020/09/24/299537.htm where a news clip was titled “Study Shows Monitoring Plus Coaching Can Cut Risky Driving in Half” shows that drivers of heavy duty vehicles, such as trucks, have a safety incentive to perform some ecodriving. Thus a nonzero value is possible. However, for the purposes of setting a baseline, the values in this input file are set to zero; the user may adjust these as more data become available.

marea_transit_fuel.html:
Optional file marea_transit_fuel.csv

May 21, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this optional file gives the transit fuel proportions for non-electric vehicles. The user does not have to include this file—it is only needed if the user wants to modify the transit fuels proportions. The first six attributes show, for vans and buses respectively, the proportion of non-electric vehicles fueled by diesel, gasoline, or compressed natural gas (CNG). The last two attributes show the proportion of non-electric rail fueled by diesel or gasoline.

For example, the input file below indicates that either Albemarle County has no bus, van, or rail service or if it does have such service, the defaults for bus, van, and rail (non-electric) fuels should be used. For Charlottesville city, all non-electric vans use diesel fuel and all non-electric buses use diesel fuel. For Charlottesville city, there either is no rail travel or the non-electric rail should use the defaults.

Note that unlike Azones or Bzones, there should be just a single Marea file when running VisionEval. For instance, consider the Charlottesville-Albemarle MPO. There will be just one Marea file. When combining these files, note that VisionEval will crash if there is a mix of numbers and NA within any of the three groups above. For example, options 1 and 2 are fine, but option 3 shown below will cause a crash.

Option 1. Each group has NA values only (this will work)

Option 2. Some groups have all NA values and others have all numbers (this will work)

Option 3. A single group has a mix of NA values and numbers (this will fail)

Note that a blank cell will perform the same as an NA value.

Possible Scenario

The main reason for using this file appears to be not to develop scenarios but rather to better quantify the impacts of certain changes—e.g., there may be a difference in terms of emissions between electrification of a fleet that runs on diesel versus electrification of a fleet that runs on gasoline. The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval mentions this input file but does not describe it further, except to say that it is optional.

marea_transit_service.html:
File 41_marea_transit_service.csv

May 29, 2026

Definition of the Input File

This file (see https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) contains 8 attributes all giving revenue miles for different forms of transit: demand-responsive (DR), vanpool (VP), regular bus (MB), rapid bus (RB), monorail or automated guideway (MG), streetcar and trolleybus (SR), light or heavy rail (HR), and commuter rail (CR). For example, suppose one is looking at the Charlottesville-Albemarle area. The data suggest that an Marea comprised of both of these counties will, in 2024 and in 2045, have 1.43 million revenue miles for paratransit (e.g., demand response) and 1.043 million revenue miles for regular bus service.

Other locations in Virginia, such as Fredericksburg, will show a value for commuter rail (CR) and those in Northern Virginia, such as Arlington and Fairfax County, will show a value for heavy rail (HR).

Possible Scenario

Changing transit service, as shown in the document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, is a substantial policy for VisionEval. That document asks “How would travel behavior change if the availability of transit were double what it is today? This topic explores the question of increasing the overall supply of transit options to a region. Transit considers both the extent to which the service is available (coverage) and the frequency of that service.” This file (marea_transit_service.csv) should be modified in conjunction with the file bzone_transit_service.csv which gives service frequency.

Method Used for Virginia

The National Transit Database was used as a starting point for these data. There are five items that users may wish to consider when applying these data in their own region. None of these are believed to be a fatal flaw at this point but may merit greater study if a user is developing a scenario highly sensitive to changes in these inputs.

The NTD is comprehensive but not complete, as it does not include transit systems that do not receive federal funds. In the past, this would have been a problem for the City of Charlottesville, which has three systems: Charlottesville Area Transit (CAT), Jaunt (a paratransit system), and the University of Virginia Transit system (UTS). In the past, only the first two might have been shown in the NTD because the UTS did not receive federal funds. In the past, this problem did not occur with another large university (Virginia Tech) because in that case, the university transit system and the city’s transit system are a single agency (Blacksburg Transit) which does receive federal funds and is in the NTD. However, it now appears that UTS operations are indeed incorporated into those with CAT, such that the NTD reporting for CAT will be complete. However, if there are other agencies in Virginia that did not receive federal funds, this could be a problem. (Note that DRPT also maintains a dashboard which appears similar to that of the NTD; see https://drpt.virginia.gov/data/performance-measures/transit-performance-data-dashboard/)

There is not always a one-to-one mapping between the locations in the NTD and the locations of service. For example, consider the Virginia Railway Express (VRE) which operates between Union Station (in Washington, D.C.) and Prince William County (one leg) and Spotsylvania (another leg). For this commuter rail system, the NTD places all 2,413,451 revenue miles from 2023 (estimated to be 2,593,603 revenue miles in 2024) in Alexandria. However, as shown by the system map for the VRE (https://www.vre.org/service/system-map/), these revenue miles do not all occur in Alexandria; rather, they occur in Alexandria, Arlington, Fairfax County, Prince William, Stafford, Manassas, Manassas Park, Spotsylvania, and Stafford. To estimate the revenue-miles for each jurisdiction, printed page 76 of the VRE financial report (https://www.vre.org/assets/1/6/Annual_Comprehensive_Financial_Report_2024.pdf) gives contributions from these agencies, and thus it was assumed that revenue-miles would be proportional to these contributions. For example, because Fairfax County contributed $5,005,547 out of a total statewide contribution of $16,000,000, Fairfax County was assigned ($5,005,547/$16,000,000)* 2,593,603 = 811,400 revenue miles.

Similarly, the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) does not have all of its miles occur in Washington but rather its miles are spread across (besides DC), suburban Maryland, Arlington, Alexandria, Fairfax County, and Loudoun. Table 6 (shown on printed page 9) of https://www.wmata.com/content/dam/wmata-com/migrated-assets/about/records/upload/fy2024-dedicated-funding-report.pdf shows contributions by agency, and these were used to allocate WMATA’s heavy rail, metrobus, and paratransit operations. This is a simplification—e.g., the above does not include Prince William County, even though WMATA provides some service (e.g., to Woodbridge) but based on another report that defines the WMATA “Transit Zone” (https://rga.lis.virginia.gov/Published/2024/RD965/PDF) this approach seems reasonable.

As with all input files, there is some judgement as to what should be the default case for the forecast year of 2045. For example, one could argue that there should be growth in transit service to the extent that there is growth in the drivers of travel demand, such as population or employment. However, because transit (as is the case with other modes) is subsidized, such an assumption also implies one should expect a continued increase in funds for transit. The research team has used a method to increase 2045 revenue miles as shown in step 3.2.6 and as shown in the corresponding Excel file should users wish to incorporate such values as a default increase. However, it a case can also be made to presume no increase in revenue miles as a base case between 2024 and 2045 (or to let regions use their own increase). Thus the corresponding CSV file has set 2045 revenue miles equal to 2024 revenue miles.

Vanpool revenue miles and bus rapid transit revenue miles are currently zero. It is probably the case that what is characterized as regular bus service in a few locations, such as Fairfax County where buses may operate free of charge in the 65 mph express lanes, could be considered bus rapid transit. Similarly there are some vanpool services in the state. If a user develops a scenario that increases the demand for these services, then it would be appropriate to experiment with the revenue miles inputs.

On balance, the second and third consideration can be minimized at the regional level, because one only needs the marea for revenue miles—that is, even though some of Charlottesville Area Transit (CAT) revenue miles are in Albemarle, this is not a fatal flaw as an analysis for that region will use the entire Marea.

model_parameters.json.html:
File 42_model_parameters.json

March 26, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/software-framework.html?q=model_parameters.json#model-directory-structure) explains that model_parameters.json stores global model parameters that may be used by multiple modules. It is intended for model-wide assumptions and should be used sparingly. In the current Virginia model, the only parameter included is the value of time (VOT), which VisionEval defines in its Concept Primer as the opportunity cost of time spent traveling. VisionEval notes that VOT is used in TimeCost calculations in the CalculateVehicleOperatingCost module.

ConceptValueNotes
Legacy baseline VOT$16/hourValue for the 2015 Sayed baseline model.
Virginia hourly income proxy$28.72/hourComputed from 2024 Virginia per-capita income divided by annual hours worked.
Whole-day weighted average assuming 0 value of personal time$5.80/hourComputed by multiplying $28.72 by the share of hours spent working; not the recommended direct VOT input.
Value of personal travel per USDOT 50% guidance$14.36/hourComputed by multiplying $28.72 by 0.5 per USDOT (2011).

Possible Scenario

One application for tuning VOT is sensitivity testing. Changing the VOT assumption changes the time-equivalent portion of generalized travel cost in VisionEval, which can affect cost comparisons across alternatives and, indirectly, model outputs that depend on perceived travel cost. A low-VOT and high-VOT sensitivity pair is possibly more defensible than treating VOT as a fixed physical constant, though this is how the parameter is treated in current VisionEval documentation.

Method Used for Virginia

Overview

We first convert Virginia 2024 per-capita income (Census) into an hourly figure using average weekly hours worked for private employees in Virginia (FRED). That produces an hourly income proxy of $28.72. Another possible candidate for VOT is obtained by multiplying that value by the share of all hours in a year spent working, yielding $5.80. A third possible value is obtained by multiplying $28.72 by 0.5 to reflect USDOT guidance for estimating the value of local personal travel.

Calculations

The first calculation is:

$50,660 / (33.9167 x 52) = $28.72 per hour

This is best interpreted as an hourly income or earnings proxy.

The second calculation is:

0.2019 x $28.72 = $5.80 per hour

This produces an average value across all hours of the year by assuming that nonworking time has zero monetary value.

The final calculation is:

$28.72 x 0.5 = $14.36 per hour

Which represents an adjusted value of personal travel time based on income in Virginia. This value is closest to the legacy value of $16 per hour included in the Sayed model, and most closely represents VisionEval’s definition of VOT as “opportunity cost of time traveled.”

Sources

VisionEval software framework documentation: https://visioneval.github.io/docs/software-framework.html?q=model_parameters.json#model-directory-structure

VisionEval concept primer, value of time (VOT): https://visioneval.github.io/docs/conceptprimer.html?q=value%20of%20time#value-of-time

U.S. Census Bureau QuickFacts, Virginia per capita income (2024): https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/VA/PST045224

FRED, Average Weekly Hours of All Employees: Total Private in Virginia (2024): https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/SMU51000000500000002

U.S. Department of Transportation, value of travel time guidance (2011 and 2016 revisions): https://www.transportation.gov/sites/dot.gov/files/docs/Value%20of%20Travel%20Time%20Memorandum.pdf

Optional File 43_other_ops_effectiveness.csv

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file is used only if one wants to “to modify the other delay effects of operations in different road classes”, however, note further that this file is not needed unless one is considering a new technology besides those mentioned in marea_operations_deployment and marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive. For example, if one is using ramp metering, one would not use this file because ramp metering is covered in marea_operations_deployment.

The values below show that no technologies beyond those noted in the other two input files (marea_operations_deployment and marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive) are being used to address recurrent or non-recurrent delay on arterials and freeways.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval mentions this input file as one of three one can use to “evaluate changes in policy and physical interventions to improve congestion through improved speed management and reduced delays.” (The other two input files are marea_operations_deployment.csv and marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive.csv).

Thus this file is potentially useful for developing a scenario where one uses technology not specified in the other two files to improve operations. For example, the Task 7.2 document describes a scenario where a “global connected vehicle program” is forecast to reduce “recurrent congested delay” by 30% and “nonrecurrent delay” by 70%. In that case, one changes the zero values shown in the yellow boxed cells to 30 and 70. One challenge with this file is defining how a technology would impact various delay levels—in this example, it is imagined that the connected vehicle program has delay reductions for the two worst delay levels (severe and extreme) but not the three better cases (no delay, moderate delay, and heavy delay).

Method Used for Virginia

For the base case, it is assumed that there are no operational tools (beyond those mentioned in the two other input files marea_operations_deployment and marea_speed_smooth_ecodrive) and thus values of 0 are presumed.

File 44_region_base_year_dvmt.csv

May 29, 2026

Definition of the Input File

This optional file (see https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) allows to adjust how heavy truck VMT and commercial service DVMT is grown, but the research team believes the following two items to be true based on experiments with this data set that are not clear from the documentation.

First, this file is required—not optional. Failure to include this file caused VE to crash.

Second, the file has two different names in the documentation: region_base_year_dvmt and region_base_year_hvytrk_dvmt.docx. The first name is the correct one.

That said, this input file does not need to be changed unless the user wants to adjust heavy truck DVMT. For example, suppose that the user notices that execution of the model for their region during the base year gives a heavy truck DVMT of 400,000. Suppose further that the user knows from previous experience that during the base year, the heavy truck DVMT is 700,000. In that case, cell C2 shown below would be changed from “NA” to “700,000”. (The values in cell B2 and D2, while logical, are not explained fully in the VisionEval documentation).

Possible Scenario

This file is not discussed in A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval which is not surprising. The same format as shown above, however, was used by Fresno (California’s) VisionEval exercise (see San Joaquin Valley VisionEval Model Documentation) except that in column C2, the authors used the heavy truck DVMT from the regional travel demand model (31.7 M).

The one reason the research team can think of for using this file is to help with model calibration. For regions that are new to VisionEval, there may be an interest in comparing VE outputs to traditional model outputs. By starting the a base year truck DVMT that derived from regional data, one can have greater confidence that other truck-related outputs in VisionEval may be specific to the region.

Method Used for Virginia

No modification to this file was performed, except to confirm that (1) the proper name is region_base_year_dvmt (changing the name caused VisionEval to crash) and (2) that placing a value in cell C2 instead of NA indeed changes the outputs (e.g., putting a number in cell C2, provided it is of course different from the input value provided by VisionEval for the base year, will yield a different DVMT in the forecast year, which can be obtained by summing the attributes HvyTrkUrbanDvmt andHvyTrkNonUrbanDvmt found within the output file named something like Region_CentralVirginia_2045 where “CentralVirginia” is the name the user has given to their VisionEval model.

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this input file is optional. It is only needed if the user wants to modify the powertrain proportion of car services. This file contains six attributes:

CarSvcAutoPropIcev: Proportion of car service automobile travel powered by internal combustion engine powertrains

CarSvcAutoPropHev: Proportion of car service automobile travel powered by hybrid electric powertrains

CarSvcAutoPropBev: Proportion of car service automobile travel powered by battery electric powertrains

CarSvcLtTrkPropIcev: Proportion of car service light truck travel powered by internal combustion engine powertrains

CarSvcLtTrkPropHev: Proportion of car service light truck travel powered by hybrid electric powertrains

CarSvcLtTrkPropBev: Proportion of car service light truck travel powered by battery electric powertrains

For example, the data below suggest that the proportion of car service automobile travel powered by internal combustion engine powertrains in Virginia in 2024 is 0.953187025, while the proportion powered by hybrid electric powertrains is 0.03204121. For each year, the values within a group must sum to 1; otherwise, VisionEval may crash.

When saving the CSV file, Excel may automatically truncate values after the ninth decimal place. Therefore, the row totals should be checked to ensure that the sum remains 1.

Possible Scenario

Changes to this file would likely be useful for analyzing the impacts of changes in the powertrain composition and vehicle mix of automobiles versus light trucks used for car service within the model region. For example, modifying the shares of ICEV, HEV, and BEV vehicles could affect outcomes related to emissions, energy consumption, fuel use, and operating costs. The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval explains that this file can be used to modify the proportion of powertrains and vehicle mix of autos vs light trucks for car service in the model region. The powertrain classifications are ICEV (internal combustion engine), HEV (hybrid electric), and BEV (battery electric) for the automobiles and light trucks used for car service. This file specifies the share of total VMT for any specific year for each of these powertrain types rather than assign specific vehicles.

Car Service Assumption: The number of car service vehicles (e.g., Uber, Lyft) is not available from any known sources. Therefore, the powertrain proportion for car service vehicles was assumed to be the same as that of registered vehicles in Virginia.

Vehicle Type Mapping: Vehicle types need to be categorized into automobiles and light trucks. However, no data source is available that provides powertrain proportions disaggregated by vehicle type. As a result, the powertrain proportions for automobiles and light trucks were assumed to be equal.

Base Year and Target Year Values Projection: At first, both the 2024 base year and the 2045 target year values were projected using the compound annual growth rate (CAGR) calculated from 2021 to 2023 data. However, the number of electric vehicles was significantly overestimated due to their high initial adoption rate.

Therefore, the total number of light-duty passenger vehicles was projected by year first, and then the number of gasoline and diesel vehicles was estimated based on the CAGR.

Given that the year-over-year increases in hybrid and electric vehicles are nearly identical, the number of new vehicles added each year was assumed to follow a 1:1 ratio between the two types. (Refer to the figure above.) Then, the number of hybrid and electric vehicles by year was estimated by subtracting the number of gasoline and diesel vehicles from the total number of light-duty vehicles, and incrementally adding an equal number of new vehicles to each category based on the previous year's values. Lastly, the proportions of each vehicle type were calculated based on the estimated numbers.

region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita.html:
Optional 49_ region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita

May 30, 2026

Definition of the Input File

There are two potential input files depending on which build is used

The VisionEval documentation mentions two files with two separate file names and two separate definitions; in both cases the file is optional. Experiments by the research team, using the multimodal module, on May 29, 2026 with a version downloaded in 2025 suggest that only the first file has an impact and thus that file is described here. However, a second file appears in the documentation and on other websites, and developers may have customized VisionEval to use this second file. The research team recommends that users either (1) decide not to use this optional file or (2) if they do use it, quickly ensure that changes in the file causes a change in outputs—that way, users do not lose time working with a file that does not affect results.

The optional file region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita is defined in the documentation at https://github.com/visioneval/VisionEval/blob/main/sources/modules/VEHouseholdVehicles/inst/module_docs/AssignDrivers.md, which users can get to by going to https://visioneval.github.io/, choose download, choose the readme file at the very bottom of the page (which takes one to https://github.com/VisionEval/VisionEval-4), then click sources, then click modules, and then click the VEHouseholdVehicles, then inst, and then module_docs, and then choose Assign_Drivers.md. Although a 2018 date is shown, it appears that this file (region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita) is indeed what is used in the current module. This file is also referenced in Incorporating Automated Vehicles into Scenario Planning Models: Phase 2 (Tool Development and Pilot Testing) by ICF for FHWA. Changes to values in this file influenced the total of household DVMT as reported in Marea 2045 sample file examined by the research team.

The optional file region_hh_driver_adjust_prop is mentioned in the documentation at https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html. This file also appears at https://visioneval.github.io/docs/validation-and-troubleshooting.html and in documentation for the Delaware Valley Regional Planning Commission (https://github.com/dvrpc/DVRPC-VisionEval-Inputs-Preparation/blob/main/documentation/Generating%20Input%20Tables/4.%20Household%20Vehicles/4.%20Household%20Vehicle.md_ and for the Fresno Council of Governments (https://www.fresnocog.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/SJV_VE_Documentation_Final.pdf). Changes to this input file did not influence the total of household DVMT. (This does not mean the file has no impact in work done for DVRPC or Fresno, as developers can customize VisionEval; it simply means that the research team, when using the standard VisionEval installation without any alterations except to use the multimodal module, did not detect any changes).

Definition of region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita

Based on the first URL mentioned in this documentation—the Assign Drivers Module, this is the ratio of “drivers to persons” in each of five age groups. For example, the data below suggest that 38.3% of persons age 15 to 19 have a driver’s license, both in 2024 and 2045. This percentage is considerably higher for the other age groups, with 89.4% of Virginians age 55 to 64 having a driver’s license in 2024 and 2045. These are the values shown in the CSV file in Table 1.

Table 1. Values Used for region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita

Definition of region_hh_driver_adjust_prop

Based on a later URL in this documentation, https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html, this file adjusts the “driver licensing rate” by age group relative to the model estimation year (which appears to be 2001). According to the documentation, the file contains five attributes, one for each age group, where a 1 indicates no adjustment.

For example, the data in Table 2 suggest that the ratio of drivers to the population age 15 to 19 in Virginia in 2024 will be higher than the same ratio for year 2001, with an adjustment factor of 1.11. By contrast, the table suggests that the ratio of drivers to population in the age 20 to 29 group in 2024, will be lower than the ratio for 2001 (with a factor of 0.63). If the ratio for licensed drivers to population were unchanged from 2001, then this file would have 1.0 in all cells. The methodology for deriving these values is given in the Appendix.

Table 2. Values for region_hh_driver_adjust_prop (detailed method described in the Appendix)

A more conservative set of changes (2001 to 2024) is shown in Table 3 and the methodology for deriving these values is given in the next section.

Table 3. Values for region_hh_driver_adjust_prop (simplified method)

Possible Scenario

Changes to this file would likely be useful for analyzing scenarios in which the model-estimated number of drivers is intentionally adjusted by age cohort to reflect observed or projected behavioral changes. For example, the file could be used to model scenarios involving declining driver licensing rates among younger populations or increasing driving participation among older populations. Such adjustments could influence model outputs related to DVMT, mode choice, household transportation costs, congestion, and emissions. The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval does not mention this input file nor licensure.

Method Used for Virginia

Region_hh_ave_driver_per_capita

Table 6.3.3. Licensed drivers, by State, sex, and age group (shown as Table DL-22 in the FHWA 2024 Highway Statistics Series (https://www.fhwa.dot.gov/policyinformation/statistics/2024/) gives the number of licensed drivers for each age group in Virginia for year 2024, and the U.S. Census Bureau (table S0101, American Community Survey, one-year estimates for 2024) gives the population by age group. (This source gives Virginia’s total 2024 population as 8,811,195; the Weldon Cooper Center for Public Service gives a total (July 1) 2025 population as being 8,880,107 (https://www.coopercenter.org/virginia-population-estimates). In short, for each of the five age groups, the number of licensed drivers was divided by the population. For example, FHWA in Table DL-22 showed 224,520 licensed drivers in 2024 and the U.S. Census Bureau (in Table S0101 from the 2024 one-year ACS) showed a Virginia population of 585,661 persons in that age group, yielding a ratio of 0.383. The same values were presumed for 2024 and 2045.

Region_hh_driver_adjust_prop (simplified method)

The values shown in Table 3 were developed using a very simple approach: the ratio of all drivers to the population for the U.S. as a whole was 0.6701 in 2001, and this ratio was 0.70796 in 2024. The ratio of these two values (e.g., 2024 to 2001) was 1.056. These values are shown in Table 3.

Appendix: How to Derive Table 2

The corresponding Excel file shows how the values for Table 2 were derived. This is a more detailed method and one that should be studied by individual regions if implemented, but an advantage is that it considers rural and urban areas differently. The extrapolation method described below was developed by comparing driver licensing rates by age cohort between urban and rural areas and calculating the relative proportions of the West Piedmont PDC region, which was assumed to represent a rural area, relative to urban areas, which were assumed to have a baseline value of 1. Therefore, the values presented in this input file are likely most appropriate for rural regions such as WPPDC.

File 51_region_prop_externalities_paid.csv

May 13, 2026

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file reflects proportional external costs for the region, including climate change and other social costs. This file contains two attributes:

PropClimateCostPaid: Proportion of climate change costs paid by users (i.e. ratio of carbon taxes to climate change costs

PropOtherExtCostPaid: Proportion of other social costs paid by users

For example, the data below suggest that the proportion of the social cost of carbon emissions borne by individuals in Virginia is 0. In addition, the proportion of the social cost of non-carbon emissions borne by individuals in Virginia—such as costs associated with motor vehicle crashes and traffic congestion—is 23%.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, does not explicitly reference this file. However, adjusting the values could intuitively affect travel behavior and transportation-related outcomes. For example, increasing the proportion of external costs borne by individuals could increase the cost of driving. As a result, the model would be expected to show changes in outcomes such as DVMT, mode choice, congestion and delay.

Method Used for Virginia

Base Year

Currently, there are no carbon-related taxes in Virginia. Although fuel taxes do exist, according to the Code of Virginia, these revenues are primarily allocated to transportation improvement and operation—not to climate change mitigation. Accordingly, the value for the base year was set to 0.

According to The Economic and Societal Impact of Motor Vehicle Crashes, 2019 (Revised February 2023), USDOT, 23.29% of the economic cost was borne by individuals ("Self"). Although this figure is based on 2019 data, it was used for both the base year (2024) and the target year (2045) due to the lack of more recent or alternative data sources. Since this value does not fully capture all other external costs, adjustments may be necessary at the discretion of the analyst, depending on future data availability or contextual needs.

Forecast Year

Regarding the target-year value for PropClimateCostPaid, no plans to introduce a carbon tax in the future were identified in any available sources. Therefore, the target-year value was also set to 0.

Regarding the PropOtherExtCostPaid value, the same value as the base year was used due to the lack of available data sources.

Definition of the Input File

VisionEval (https://visioneval.github.io/docs/model-inputs.html) explains that this file contains different types of road costs. This file contains six attributes:

RoadBaseModCost: Average base modernization cost per light-duty vehicle mile traveled (dollars per vehicle mile). Base modernization includes roadway improvements exclusive of addition of lanes.

RoadPresOpMaintCost: Average road preservation, operations, and maintenance cost per light-duty vehicle mile traveled (dollars per vehicle mile).

RoadOtherCost: Average other road cost (e.g. administration, planning, project development, safety) per light-duty vehicle mile traveled (dollars per vehicle mile).

FwyLnMiCost: Average cost to build one freeway lane-mile (dollars per lane-mile)

ArtLnMiCost: Average cost to build one arterial lane-mile (dollars per lane-mile)

HvyTrkPCE: Passenger car equivalent (PCE) for heavy trucks. PCE indicates the number of light-duty vehicles a heavy truck is equivalent to in calculating road capacity.

For example, the data below suggest that the average base modernization cost per light-duty vehicle mile traveled in 2024 is 0.0258451 dollars per vehicle mile in 2022 dollars. In addition, the average cost to build one freeway lane-mile in 2024 is 10,344 dollars per lane-mile in 2018 dollars. The same values were applied in 2045 because it was assumed that there would be no increase beyond inflation.

Possible Scenario

The document Task 7.2 Simplified Scenario Development guide, available at A Playbook for Simplified Approaches for Creating Scenarios in VisionEval, does not explicitly reference this file. This appendix examines how input variable values—specifically in region_road_cost.csv—should be entered in terms of the appropriate currency year. The Sayed model presents an example using region_road_cost.csv, in which the base year is 2019, and the three variables (RoadBaseModCost.2005, RoadPresOpMaintCost.2005, RoadOtherCost.2005) appear to use cost values denominated in 2005 dollars. Relevant Module: BalanceRoadCostsAndRevenues

Input Format Logic: According to the module documentation for BalanceRoadCostsAndRevenues, users are allowed to specify the year of currency directly within the field name. Specifically, when the TYPE is set to "currency", the field name must be followed by a period and the year the values are denominated in. This implies that users do not need to manually convert currency values to the model’s base year (e.g., 2005), as the system handles that internally.

NAME - The field (column) name in the input file. Note that if the 'TYPE' is 'currency' the field name must be followed by a period and the year that the currency is denominated in. For example if the NAME is 'HHIncomePC' (household per capita income) and the input values are in 2010 dollars, the field name in the file must be 'HHIncomePC.2010'. The framework uses the embedded date information to convert the currency into base year currency amounts. The user may also embed a magnitude indicator if inputs are in thousand, millions, etc. The VisionEval model system design and users guide should be consulted on how to do that.

Conclusion: Input variable names can be updated to reflect the actual year of the cost values provided (e.g., RoadBaseModCost.2022). This approach allows the model to apply the necessary deflation logic internally and avoids unnecessary manual adjustments.
